speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. For the election of 1979, 18 new members of Parliament were added to the House of Commons, increasing the total from 264 to 282. After this week's census has been completed the House will grow by another 30 members, if the provisions of the Representation Act, 1974, are left as they are now.
Since the chamber has reached the limit of its capacity, since the cost of 30 more members of Parliament will be extremely high, and because many in this chamber feel it is already difficult enough to participate fully in the Question Period and the procedures of the House, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the provisions of the Representation Act, 1974, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, and that the government assist the committee by preparing a background paper setting out possible alternatives to the endless and unnecessary expansion of the size of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent for this motion?
Agreed.

NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS FAIR DISTRIBUTION OF WEALTH AMONG ALL NATIONS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter which may have the support of all parties in the House. It concerns the death of Dame Barbara Ward, who devoted her life to a fairer distribution of the world's resources between rich and poor nations. In view of the upcoming summit meeting in Ottawa where the North-South question might be pursued, and in view of the serious consequences that inaction will bring about for people in the developing regions of the world, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That this House express its renewed commitment to the cause of a fair distribution of wealth among all nations of the world.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent necessity. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the present economic situation in Canada baffles him. He cannot understand why people keep borrowing money, with such high interest rates. Surely the Prime Minister could try to

June 1, 1981
5.0.	43
understand the problems of small business. With the high rate of inflation, high rents, wages and all other aspects of small business, it simply becomes a matter of survival. They must borrow, no matter what the rate is, in order to avoid bank-rukptcy a little longer, hoping that someone in government will come to their senses and help them. But either the government does not care-and I hope that is not the case-or it does not understand small business. Assuming the latter, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That this House direct the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to contact an organization such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen and meet with them in order to learn how it really is in small business in Canada today.

subsubtopic: ECONOMIC POLICY OF ALBERTA PREMIER-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Despite the fact that inflation is the No. 1 problem in Canada today, the Premier of Alberta has adopted two pro-inflationary moves in the past week, the first being a cutback of oil supplies to the east and the second being his advocating loose money supply and
increased spending. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield):
That this House request the Premier of Alberta to reconsider his pro-inflationary policy and join the battle against inflation by stopping his cutback of oil to the east and by ceasing to advocate inflationary spending.

subsubtopic: STEPS TO AVOID POSSIBILITY OF STRIKE-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Once again threats of postal disruptions are being heard in Canada. At a time when the Post Office is being turned into a Crown corporation, which we are told may hopefully solve some of these problems, many small business people who rely on the postal system for their livelihood are justifiably concerned, as are millions of Canadians who are fed up with the constant labour problems connected with the Post Office. Since the labour contract expired last December and contract talks have been going on for months now, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That this House urge the President of the Treasury Board and the president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers to settle their differences immediately, thus avoiding chaos in Canada and ensuring mail delivery to Canadians who pay for and deserve continuing service.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Given the fact that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) has failed to acknowledge the serious economic problems faced by the west coast fishing industry due to declining stock levels, excess fleet capacity, and haphazard management practices, together with the compounding impact on fishermen of the Liberal government's high interest rate policies, and given the fact that the government on Friday last rejected my motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 calling for a special House order to authorize the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to visit the west coast during the month of June to investigate these serious problems firsthand, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That this House instruct the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to make an immediate statement on motions outlining the steps he will take to alleviate the threat of bankruptcy and vessel seizure faced by hundreds of west coast Fishermen to prevent a collapse of the west coast fishing industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of any of the leading members of the government-as a matter of fact there are only 14 cabinet ministers here out of 32. Fourteen! That is how concerned they are about the events today. Fifteen! One just joined us. The Prime Minister is not here, the Minister of Finance is not here-

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext:
Where's Joe?

June 1, 1981
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is to ask a question, not make a speech about who is present in the House.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext:
My question, Madam Speaker, in light of this indifference of the government, is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The director of the Economic Council of Canada, Dr. Slater, spoke before the House of Commons finance committee on Friday. He said that a mix of policies is the best way to fight inflation, and that no single policy can cure inflation. He then said that Governor Bouey has been left by the government to go it alone to fight inflation with monetary policy only. The government has no other anti-inflation policy in effect.
In view of this criticism by the official economic advisory Council to the government, of the government's lack of policy, does the government plan to resign? Does it plan to ask the Minister of Finance to resign to put in a minister who will bring in policies, or does the government plan to introduce some anti-inflationary policies to help the people of this country and to help Mr. Bouey in his anti-inflation campaign?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think that the hon. member's question, quoting the chairman of the Economic Council, confirms that we are doing exactly what the chairman said we should do, and that is to pursue a mix of policies of an appropriate nature. This, in fact, is the approach of the government. In the last budget the Minister of Finance pointed out how, as part of an effort to restrain the forces of inflation, we are following, for example, a policy of expenditure restraint. So I think that we are doing something quite consistent with the advice of the chairman of the Economic Council, and where there are further initiatives to be announced, my colleague, the Minister of Finance, will be very quick to announce them.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: I am glad that the minister agrees with what Dr. Slater has been saying, because Dr. Slater said the fight against inflation being waged by the government is little more than a phony war.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ANTI-INFLATION POLICIES
speechtext: That is what the director of the Economic Council of Canada thinks. That is the mix of policies that the government has, the phony war.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Dr. Slater said some of the policies which would be helpful would be an energy agreement on prices and revenue sharing, but there is nothing like that yet; a fiscal arrangement with the provinces which is in line with the present situation; and an investment strategy and program for the country.
The minister is supposed to be the author of the great investment strategy. We have not seen it yet. The deficit has not been reduced, though it is stated to be a plan. Can the minister tell us when are we going to have action in any of those areas which might help the battle against inflation? When? Specifically, if he cannot answer with reference to the rest, when is the minister's mighty mountain of an industrial strategy going to come mouse-like forward from the minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, through numerous announcements we have been making in the area of industrial policy, we are confirming that we are moving in the right directions for the Canadian economy when it comes to industrial policy.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Also, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, is working very hard to get the right kind of energy agreement with the producing provinces, which is something that the government of my hon. friends opposite was totally incapable of doing in spite of being in bed with the governments of the producing provinces. After listening to my hon. friend's questions, I understand very well why the Leader of the Opposition could not even get up the courage to come in and hear those questions. They certainly are not worth being present for, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a final supplementary question. This government is so interested in the affairs of Canada that 15 of 32 cabinet ministers show up in the House! There is no external affairs, no defence, no finance, no Prime Minister! You are the government! If you want to give us your portfolios, we will show up.
My final supplementary to the minister is this. The minister and his-
Oh, oh!
Madam Speaker, they do not like their neglect pointed out to the public.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Order, please.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The minister has had 15 months to bring forward an industrial policy. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has had 15 months to reach an agreement with the provinces and all he has done is put forward conditions that no one can accept, and it has stalemated our whole energy investment and recovery program. Will the minister tell us what the timetable is for achieving completion of these strategies and putting them into action so that the battle against inflation can start to be
June 1, 1981

successful? When are they going to have a sense of urgency? When are they going to act to help the Canadians who are suffering so badly today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all I should point out that I understand the Prime Minister is taking part in a meeting of the Council of Maritime Premiers, and that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is accompanying the Governor General on an important mission to Scandinavia. I hope that this is not something that my hon. friend would see fit to oppose, or object to.
He is having a sauna. Where is the Minister of Finance? He came on the plane last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think the evidence is clear that we are working vigorously to achieve progress, and that we have achieved progress in the areas my hon. friend has mentioned. If he is serious about what he is saying, he would do more than he has to make sure that we get the necessary co-operation, in particular from the producing provinces, in the energy area.
With respect to the number of ministers at present in the House, I might say that those who are here are more than enough to deal with the vapid and empty questions of the opposition.

Madam Speaker, I have two supplementary questions to put to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the lack of an energy policy and the impact this is having on inflation and economic growth in the country.
Government policy in Canada has contributed to a surge in profits in the refining and retailing side of the energy business, causing Canadians to pay much more than is necessary for energy in this country. Let me quote an example. As a result of the deregulation of oil prices in the United States, Gulf Oil in the U.S. went from a profit of $247 million in the first quarter of 1980 to a loss of $186 million in the first quarter of 1981. That is in the downstream side of the business. At the same time Gulf Canada went from a $55 million profit to a $95 million profit this year. In light of this, what does the minister propose specifically to remedy the situation? How is he learning from what is going on in the United States, in the evolution of his energy policy for this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all my hon. colleague has forgotten to point out that he has at heart the welfare of consumers. He should have indicated in his question, since he likes to refer to the United States' experience, that at the present time the American consumer is paying about 50 cents per gallon more than the Canadian consumer. We in this country have tried to protect the Canadian consumer from the inflationary impact of the very high price of gasoline. In all honesty, my friend should have referred to that.
Oral Questions
He refers to some profit situation with regard to particular firms. I would suggest to my hon. friend that his party should get their energy act together because, for the last six months, what we have heard from the other side has been that a National Energy Program was going to destroy the oil industry in this country.
It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: They say it is, and at the same time their official spokesman accuses us of letting corporations make high profits. Make up your minds, fellows.

Madam Speaker, the minister quite rightly points out what has happened in the United States. Let me quote the consumer price index figures which show that in July, 1980, Canada had a lower consumer price index growth, 10.1 per cent, against 13.1 per cent relative to the United States. This year the whole thing has turned around. We are now 2.6 percentage points higher, for a deterioration in the inflation performance in Canada relative to the United States of 5.6 per cent in less than a year. That is what is happening in this country, and the minister should listen to that.
Let me be quite specific in my supplementary question. Part of the Gulf Canada increased profits results from the paper profits that the minister referred to in this House a couple of months ago. These are caused by the minister through the imposition of his petroleum compensation charge, the Canadian ownership charge, and the Lalonde levy which result in real price increases to the consumer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. That question is a bit long. I would ask the hon. member to try to shorten it.

I was just coming to the question, Madam Speaker. The point is that what the consumer loses, the government gains by income tax increases. Since I indicated, in a letter dated April 17 to the minister, that the problem could be remedied easily by a minor change in the method of imposing that tax, what action is the minister taking as a result of my letter to save Canadians in excess of $170 million in taxes which go to his government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as far as the point raised by the hon. member with regard to inflation rates is concerned, because we were able to keep energy prices at a lower level last year, in particular, we have been able to maintain our inflation rate lower than that in the United States.
That is wrong.

Last year.

June 1, 1981
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Last year; last July. That is what I said. As far as this year is concerned, if I were to listen to the official opposition, we would have even higher inflation rates-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -because what these gentlemen and ladies in the Conservative party are recommending is higher prices to the consumer than are in evidence at the present time. This is what we, on this side, have been fighting against. We have been trying to get an arrangement so as to continue protecting the Canadian consumer while providing adequate returns to the industry.
How do you justify the PetroCan tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: As far as the last point raised by the hon. member is concerned, I have had an opportunity to discuss this issue with him. He knows that the situation is not as simple as he wants to make it appear, and as a consequence I do not intend to make changes to the present policy.

subsubtopic: MANDATORY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAMS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, moving on to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who is also the minister responsible for the status of women, can he now confirm that he fully supports mandatory affirmative action employment programs for women and other disadvantaged groups, including contract compliance? When will the minister recommend to cabinet the immediate implementation of them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: MANDATORY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAMS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have indicated all along that we are prepared to take a wide variety of measures to improve substantially the equality of women in the work place. We have introduced a number of them during the past year, including new training programs, an affirmative action program in the public service, as well as the opening of new counselling centres. I have indicated that we are hoping to present in Parliament, in a matter of two or three weeks, a wide variety of recommendations and proposals dealing with changes in the labour and employment market in Canada, which will include a number of measures which will substantially benefit the working women in this country. I would ask the hon. member to restrain her impatience and see those recommendations in total so that we can have an entire strategy instead of just one or two measures.

subsubtopic: MANDATORY AFFIRMATIVE ACTION PROGRAMS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: You always say that to women.

Madam Speaker, that is a most disappointing answer, particularly in light of the letter I received from the minister on Friday which said that he would be approaching cabinet soon with a proposal respecting mandatory affirmative action, which is what my question was all about, not these other vague programs.
A recent document prepared for cabinet by the minister has also just come to my attention which states that what the minister is calling for is not mandatory action but voluntary action, voluntary affirmative action and voluntary contract compliance in the private sector. A memorandum last year dated May 21, 1980, from the minister's own department stated:
-four years of experience with a voluntary federal contracts program produced no results.
Why is the minister reversing himself?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is becoming convoluted in the wealth of her own speculations. I simply suggest to her that the commitment of this government to improve substantially the place of women and the equality of women in the work place is one which is well recognized. We will continue that commitment. We will have a number of recommendations that she, her colleagues, and many other people in this country might, and I hope will, support.

The
minister has totally reversed himself from May of last year to just the other day, as this document which was leaked to us shows. Finally, I ask the minister whether he will reconsider the key to providing greater equality in the work place, which is mandatory affirmative action and mandatory contract compliance? Will he consider taking this diluted document, throwing it out, replacing it with the one he prepared only a year ago, and presenting that to cabinet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to caution the hon. member to place very little confidence in leaked documents that come by way of brown paper bags from moles they have inside some parts of the public service. The fact is that we are considering a wide variety of recommendations. As soon as they are completed, finalized and presented where all members of Parliament will see them, we can get into an honest debate.
June 1, 1981

subsubtopic: CANADIAN COMPANIES INVOLVED IN LITIGATION IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My question is directed to the Minister of Justice. It arises out of an answer given by the Prime Minister last Friday when asked by the hon. member for York-Peel when the gag regulations were going to be rescinded. The Prime Minister at that time said:
There are still some cases before the courts now, some Canadian citizens and some Canadian corporations are still sought after by American law. We will protect them as long as is necessary,-
Can the minister specify what Canadian companies or individuals are involved in litigation in the United States? What are the projections for termination of that litigation and, consequently, when are these gag regulations going to be removed so that Canadians can understand the facts of this sordid mess?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: CANADIAN COMPANIES INVOLVED IN LITIGATION IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not have anything to add to the answer given by the Prime Minister last week. The hon. member is asking for a very precise answer which I do not have at this moment. I do not know if I can make it public. The Prime Minister stated the government's policy on Friday. We have to protect Canadian interests with regard to actions carried out in Canada and not according to the laws of other nations. We must ensure that the laws which control Canadian industries and citizens are Canadian laws, not American.

Madam Speaker, I am surprised that the Minister of Justice does not know what litigation is in progess now because it is the underpinning upon which the Prime Minister says he is maintaining these gag regulations.
Why is the government protecting and sheltering Canadian companies potentially in violation of American price fixing laws? If the shoe were on the other foot and American companies were being protected by an American government, would this government not be complaining and screaming?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
The hon. member is asking a hypothetical question. We would have to deal with the serious situation at that time to ensure that action in Canada regarding an international situation was done according to international law. subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-PROVISIONS IN MAIN ESTIMATES, 1981-82
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the Chair several votes in the Main Estimates, 1981-82 which I believe to be out of order and inappropriate for inclusion in the subsequent appropriations bill flowing from these estimates.
The general argument in regard to whether votes in the estimates are in order or out of order was made by myself as recently as March 24 of this year and by numerous members in the House going back to 1971. Arguments have been made repeatedly over the last decade that votes should deal only with the appropriation of funds and not seek to amend legislation. They have been the subject of several rulings by the Chair.
June 1, 1981

I do not think I am being presumptive in saying that the position of the Chair in respect to this dollar item issue, as it has been titled, is very, very clear. March 25, 1981, was the most recent time this subject came up in regard to Supplementary Estimates (C), 1980-81. At that time Madam Speaker quoted Mr. Speaker Jerome who on March 22, 1977, probably stated it as precisely as in any ruling of the Chair when he said:
-the government receives from Parliament the authority to act through the passage of legislation and receives the money to finance such authorized action through the passage by Parliament of an appropriation act. A supply item in my opinion ought not, therefore, to be used to obtain authority which is the proper subject of legislation-
So it is very clear. Therefore, in order to prove that votes should be struck down as being out of order, it is simply necessary to show that they go beyond appropriation funds and somehow seek authority from Parliament for the government to undertake action.
On the last occasion I brought this up, on March 24, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston)-it may have been spontaneous-resorted to the argument that an appropriation act is legislation and, therefore, it is fine to use an appropriation act for legislative purposes. As I indicated, that argument has been made repeatedly over the last decade and struck down by the Speaker every time. I will not go over that ground again, but I put the caveat that if perchance the President of the Treasury Board should make those arguments in a way as to be persuasive and cause the Chair to reconsider these clearly established rulings thus far, I would ask the Chair's indulgence to participate in any such debate if it should arise.
I will not take the time of the House to go over the reasons for the Chair's rulings. I will operate under the assumption that the ruling is clear and precise, and I will bring the various votes to your attention as to their eligibility or whether or not they are in order.
First I refer the House to vote 30 in the Department of Agriculture, page 2-26 of the Main Estimates, 1981-82. This vote is tantamount to an amendment to the Animal Disease and Protection Act. In essence, vote 30 indicates that, notwithstanding the restrictions of the Animal Disease and Protection Act in respect of conditions which must be satisfied in order for compensation to be paid, payment is authorized, even when the conditions of the act are not met. In other words, vote 30 seeks to amend the Animal Disease and Protection Act. The vote comprises the following:
Contributions including compensation at rates determined in the manner provided by Section 12 of the Animal Disease and Protection Act to owners of animals affected with diseases under that act that have died or have been slaughtered in circumstances not covered by the act.
This vote would seek to extend the provisions of the act to situations not covered by the act. This is the precise language, it is clearly legislating. I would consider it to be out of order.
Next I refer the Chair to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, pages 7-12 and 7-14, votes 35, 40 and 45. In essence, each of these votes seeks parliamentary authority to establish new programs. Vote 35 deals with the Canadian
Point of Order-Mr. Andre
home insulation program. In the commencement of that vote, the exact language indicates that it provides for the following:
Contributions in respect of a home insulation program in the provinces of-
Then it goes on. It talks about "a", not "the". In other words, it is establishing a new home insulation program.
Later in the description of the vote, it asks for authority to be provided to the governor in council to make regulations in respect of this program. The vote is seeking authority, on behalf of the governor in council or on behalf of the government, to make regulations in respect of the home insulation program which the vote seeks to create.
Vote 40 is precisely the same in respect of the home insulation program or the so-called HIP which concerns provinces other than those included under CHIP.
Vote 45 on page 7-14 deals with the Canadian oil substitution program. It seeks authority to establish this program and it also seeks authority for the governor in council to make regulations in respect to that authority. Presumably, if these programs were in existence by some legislative authority the votes would have read "contributions for the Canadian home insulation program", "contributions for the home insulation program", or "contributions for the Canadian oil substitution program". The votes go much beyond that and give authority to the governor in council to make regulations, and so on and so forth. They do not talk about the CHIP program, the HIP program or the COSP program; they talk about "a" program. The language is very clear; the intent is for Parliament to give authority to the government to do that.
In any case, I have been unable to discover any other place where authority for these programs could be obtained. To my knowledge there has been no legislation establishing these programs, nor is there any existing legislation which would give the government authority to undertake these programs. I have not been able to discover that, but perhaps I could be enlightened to the contrary if that is the situation.
I next refer the Chair to votes L45, L50, L55 and L60 under the "External Affairs" estimates found at pages 9-30 and 9-32. Each of these votes seeks authority for the governor in council to issue certain debt instruments, namely, non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes. For example, the Chair will note in vote L45 it is stated:
-to confirm and ratify the issue of non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes to international financial institutions for international development assistance in previous years in an amount of $169,177,325.
In other words, this vote seeks to confirm and ratify the issuance of these debt instruments. The other votes, vote L50, L55 and L60, are, in fact, for one dollar. They are in the classical one dollar mode, if you will. A vote for a dollar is clearly not seeking funds but the authority to undertake certain action. Your Honour's predecessors, and perhaps Your Honour as well, have ruled that a dollar item may be appropriate in amending previous appropriations acts, that is, transferring money from one vote to another which may have been authorized in a previous appropriations act. But a dollar item

June 1, 1981
Point of Order-Mr. Andre
is not appropriate for granting legislative authority to the government. The dollar items here mention no such previous appropriations act. They are not an attempt to transfer funds from one vote to another; they are an attempt to grant the government authority to undertake certain actions.
The reason the authority is needed to undertake what is being undertaken arises from the Financial Administration Act. Section 80 of the Financial Administration Act states:
Except as provided in this act or any other act of the Parliament of Canada,
(a)	a Crown debt is not assignable and
(b)	no transaction purporting to be an assignment of a Crown debt is
effective so as to confer on any person any rights or remedies in respect to
such debt.
Section 79 of the Financial Administration Act defines "Crown debt" as any debt for which the Crown is or may become liable.
In each of these votes the authority is sought to issue a demand note, which is a Crown debt. It could confer on the Crown or impose an obligation on the Crown to make payment on that note when it is demanded by the holders of the note, which are various international agencies. The Financial Administration Act says that can be done only with legislative authority, authority from Parliament. Hence, these votes in the estimates for a dollar seek that authority. That authority is not permissible under the rulings made by Your Honour and Your Honour's predecessor. Therefore, I submit all of these votes are out of order and should be struck down.
1 refer the Chair next to the Department of Finance estimates on page 10-28, vote L15, which is precisely the same as the votes I mentioned previously. It is a dollar vote to authorize the minister to issue non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes in such form as the minister may determine. In other words, all of the arguments I provided with respect to the votes under the Department of External Affairs estimates may be applied to the votes under the Department of Finance estimates. That is to say, the Financial Administration Act would prohibit the government from doing that without legislative authority. The government should not seek legislative authority through the appropriations bill to do that through a dollar item.
I next refer the Chair to page 23-64, Department of Public Works estimates, vote L70, which again is a dollar item. On examination of the vote it becomes clear that the intention of this vote is to amend legislation. It is merely for a dollar; therefore it does not seek funds. The purpose of the vote is to amend sections 34.14(2)(a) and (b) and section 40(5)(a) and (b) of the National Housing Act.
1 next refer the Chair to page 29-12, Department of Supply and Services estimates, vote 5. It is stated under vote 5:
-an amount not exceeding $3,020,000 in respect of the costs of free and subsidized publications shall not be taken into account in the calculation of the expenditures referred to in subsection 29(3) of the Adjustment of Accounts Act.
In other words, this vote clearly seeks to amend subsection 29(3) of the Adjustment of Accounts Act, which unamended would prohibit the government from undertaking this activity. I submit vote 5 is also out of order.
Finally, I refer Your Honour to vote 110, Department of Transport estimates, page 30-90. I would like to quote from line six of that vote:
-provide that subsection 6(2) of the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act shall not apply in the case of the payment of assistance in the current fiscal year to truckers pursuant to subsection 6(1) of that act.
This vote clearly seeks to amend the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, something which is not permissible. According to the rulings of the Chair, votes cannot be used to amend legislation.
Those are the only votes I intend to seek a ruling on. I humbly submit that each of the votes I have mentioned is out of order, given the clarity of the Chair's decisions in respect of what can or cannot be included in an appropriations bill arising from the estimates. I have the suspicion, Madam Speaker, that there are a great number of other votes in the estimates which may also be out of order. To be frank, I lack the resources to do the research necessary to confirm one way or another whether this is so. I do not have the back-up staff which the President of the Treasury Board has to make that kind of assessment.
After ten years of raising this point of order I am astounded that this same question has come up repeatedly year after year. The Chair has not been ambiguous but, rather, very precise and proper in its rulings, yet year after year when the main or supplementary estimates are before us they contain items which are clearly out of order to any fair-minded person. Frankly, it is bordering on contempt of Parliament. In fact, the regularity of the Chair's decisions in respect of the order of propriety of these items are just dismissed. The Chair's rulings seem not to matter one whit when preparation is commenced in terms of the next set of estimates. They just carry on. If some get struck down, that is just too bad; they just put in a new set the next go around.
It is getting to the point where I am wondering whether we perhaps should not entertain a new procedure of handling this. Heretofore, the responsibility, if you will, has rested upon the opposition to examine these estimates and to make our position known to the Chair; the Chair has examined the arguments and ruled one way or another. I do not mean in any way, shape or form to be critical of the Chair. I think the Chair has been quite lenient toward the government in the past by saying that though it has been suspicious about certain items, it would leave them there for now, but in the future it would have to be shown that they are in order. That kind of warning seems not to have had any effect.
I am therefore going to offer the suggestion that we might look at another arrangement whereby members of Parliament can raise points of order in respect of votes, and they will be deemed out of order until such time as the government proves, to the satisfaction of the Chair, that they are in order, rather than the reverse. I agree that that opens the possibility for abuse; but we have had ten years of abuse of Parliament from the government by its total neglect and disregard of decisions
June 1, 1981

and rulings of the Chair in respect to what is appropriate for an appropriations act and what is appropriate for legislation.
I would ask the Chair to give this some consideration. It would be an awful lot easier for all of those people in the Bell tower to present argument justifying their actions than for some of us on this side to have to rely on our modest staffs to go through this horrendous document to find out whether, in fact, the votes are appropriate or merely a sneaky manner in which to try to obtain legislative authority for undertaking their actions.
Madam Speaker, I do not want to take up any more time of the House. I would ask Your Honour to give serious considerations to those votes and, perhaps, to the suggestion as to how we may handle this in the future, because ten years is enough time for anyone to learn, even the group opposite.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-PROVISIONS IN MAIN ESTIMATES, 1981-82
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in presenting his point of order, the hon. member makes much of the fact that this has been going on for ten years, with regularity, he suggests. I point out to him that, if anything, the objections have been ruled inapplicable with regularity, and in very few instances have there actually been deletions of items. In a moment, I would like to review with the House some of the instances in which such deletions have taken place.
The hon. member also very wisely, I might say, anticipated an argument which he is clearly incapable of answering; that is, the fact that what we have here is an appropriation act, an act of Parliament. He tends to reject that argument out of hand, and yet that has been the basis of many of the decisions by Speakers in the past. When this act is approved, it comes into force like any other act. While appropriation acts themselves are not subject to debate in this House, in accordance with the Standing Orders, they nevertheless cover the nonstatutory items contained in estimates which are scrutinized by the standing committees of the House.
In the case of main estimates, as we all know, the period of time for committees to review the spending plans and to call witnesses is three months. I suggest that those three months should provide ample time to discuss the items, particularly those items which may be of concern to hon. members, such as the $1 items to which the hon. member has made reference.
The second point I would like to make relates to the types of votes. My comments concern those types of votes which have been questioned by hon. members over time, and which have resulted in some items being disallowed by Your Honour's predecessors from time to time. In reviewing those items, I noted that the votes which were disallowed contained requests to amend provisions of other acts, particularly where those changes were of a continuing nature and would not appear in the Statutes of Canada. I agree that estimates should not normally be used to change the basic purpose or intent of existing legislation. However, it should be appreciated that these proposals are not always straightforward. In many cases, this is the reason for debate.
Point of Order-Mr. Andre
I believe we have made every effort to follow this general guideline, and I suggest that we have been successful in this respect. The items which were allowed by previous Speakers were financially related and provided for expenditures of money, which is the purpose of appropriation acts.
Turning to a third point concerning the $1 votes objected to by the hon. member during the review of supplementary estimates (C), they contain requests for deletion of debts, which Your Honour may recall you disallowed, for loan guarantees and for authority to invest in international development banks, which Your Honour allowed to stand.
With regard to loan guarantees which are included in appropriation acts, it should be noted that they are one time in nature, financially related; hence, on the basis of previous rulings, the estimates would appear to be the proper vehicle for obtaining parliamentary approval. In any case, if there is default, the resulting expenditure will appear in estimates and public accounts.
With respect to investments in the International Development Bank, there are four such votes in the 1981-82 Main Estimates. These votes would authorize the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to sign notes for a one-year period within a total commitment made by the government. In most cases, the cash requirements of the notes signed in a specific year fall due over a number of years, with the results that the cash requirement in the same year from the authority requested for a specific note is less than the note to be signed. The cash requirement for this note and from previous notes signed are displayed in estimates as "statutory" so that the government's spending plan contains the cash outlays for the fiscal year in question. I would also like to point out that these items are specifically defined investments which make them truly financial in nature, and that they are similar to other nonbudgetary. loan and investment votes.
In conclusion, I would like to say that I appreciate the concerns of the hon. member; but I would reiterate that the items contained in the Main Estimates which he has attacked, are financially oriented. They do not change the essence of other acts and, in my view, they are proper items to be included in these estimates and the resulting Appropriation Act. The hon. member makes specific reference, for example, to certain votes of Energy, Mines and Resources, certain program votes. Of course, legislation will be introduced with respect to these programs.
In summary, where authority is given through an appropriation act, then it would seem entirely appropriate to amend that authority through another appropriation act. Where there is an amendment effectively to other statutes, then I suggest, provided it does not go to the intent or purpose of that statute but simply to the financial provisions or a change in financial provisions, then that would also be an appropriate way in which to effect that change; namely, through an appropriation act.

Point of Order-Mr. Andre
Madam Speaker, I draw your attention for a moment to the disallowance of some items in supplementary estimates (c), in order to indicate the dilemma in which I find myself and to seek your guidance with respect to what steps you would consider appropriate.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, that eight items in supplementary estimates (c) cancelled debts and you ruled that they were pure legislative item seeking to amend section 18(1) of the Financial Administration Act. You ruled "that they should be and are hereby deleted from supplementary estimates (c) 1981-82". That was your ruling on March 25, 1981, Madam Speaker.
In the past we have always used these $1 items to delete such debts. Section 18(1) of the Financial Administration Act provides as follows:
The governor in council, on the recommendation of Treasury Board, may make regulations authorizing deletion from the accounts, in whole or in part, of any obligation or debt due to Her Majesty or any claim by Her Majesty that does not exceed five thousand dollars.
You can see, Madam Speaker, that it is not necessary to resort to legislation but simply to regulations to effect a deletion of debts up to $5,000. The question is, then, what procedures should the government adopt to delete debts which exceed that limit? I suggest, Madam Speaker, that this requires legislation and it occurred to us that the appropriate legislation would be an appropriation act. If not an appropriation act, Madam Speaker, I ask what kind of legislation would be appropriate? Perhaps an omnibus bill of some kind but it is clearly important that these come to the attention of members of the House and that is precisely why they are provided as one dollar items.
I would conclude, Madam Speaker, that the precedents we have followed in the preparation of the main estimates fully justify the items which have been attacked by the hon. member. 1 would hope that you would confirm that the main estimates have been properly prepared in accordance with precedent.

4.	There are three forms of tax incentives available to the private sector for expenditures on R&D.
(i)	The 100 per cent write-off
Since 1961, firms have been able to write off against income 100 per cent of current and capital expenditures on R & D, less government grants and tax credits applicable to such expenditures. This is an incentive since all R&D expenditures are of a capital nature (i.e., designed to yield future income) and the normal treatment would be to capitalize such expenditures and depreciate them over the economic life of the assets acquired.
(ii)	The investment tax credit
Since March, 1977, current and capital R&D expenditures have been eligible for the investment tax credit. This now stands at 10 per cent except in the Gaspe and the Atlantic Provinces, where a 20 per cent rate applies, and 25 per cent for small business anywhere in Canada.
(iii)	The research allowance
Since April, 1978, firms undertaking R&D expenditures have been eligible to deduct from income 50 per cent of the amount by which the present year's current and capital R&D expenditures exceed the average of the past three years.
5.	Research and development as an activity is a complex process whose outcome is subject to varying degrees of uncertainty. R&D by its very nature is best viewed as an investment which has an expected pay-off mainly in the longer run and, for the individual company or industry, these pay-offs may not be realized for ten to fifteen years. Hence, the relationship between any given level of increase in R&D expenditures and its impact on the economy is both indirect and imprecise. Nevertheless, the results of various studies undertaken both in Canada and other industrial nations indicate that the contribution of R&D to economic growth and productivity is positive, significant and high.
Studies have shown that the returns from R&D investment have also been significant. At the industry or company level, some typical rates of return that have been calculated for specific industries are: chemicals, 30 to 50 per cent; petroleum, 40 per cent; and food, apparel and furniture, 15 per cent.
Moreover, those industries which purchase goods embodying innovations developed by others also benefit from R&D activities. This diffusion of technology serves to strengthen the economy generally by increasing the over-all level of productivity, thereby contributing to increased standards of living.
It is now generally recognized that the expanding industries of today tend to be those industries in which the rate of investment in R&D is relatively high. A recent MOSST study for example confirmed that, for the period 1961 to 1974, research-intensive industries significantly outperformed low-research-intensive industries by recording a higher rate of growth in output, employment and productivity and a lower rate of price increases.

June 1, 1981
Order Paper Questions
able to determine that 10,000 refugees in the Peruvian embassy were nothing but a bunch of thieves, prostitutes and criminals. This was pretty fast work in two hours.
The last question that I would like to ask why it has not been answered is one for which I do not have the number in front of me but I am sure the parliamentary secretary will be familiar with it. This is a question about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) going to Jamaica and accepting as a host Sir Harold Mitchell, chief executive and director of Luscar Ltd. a large coal enterprise in western Canada. I asked if the Prime Minister had followed the guidelines that he and his government set down, namely, that any benefit of a value exceeding $200 must be reported. That question has been on the Order Paper for one year and one month and is unanswered. It would seem to me that it would be a simple thing to answer that. Apparently the Prime Minister has gone back and accepted such hospitality again.
He drew up the guidelines, Madam Speaker. None of us can do anything, if we are over there in the seats of the mighty, over $200, yet he is apparently not following his own guidelines. I want to know why. Why will he not tell us? Obviously it is embarrassing or it would not have taken over a year to get an answer.
Those are the questions that I would like to draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. If he could possibly tell us now when some of them will be answered, it would be helpful. I hope he will not give us the percentages of how many he has answered of mine and how many come through every day, how wonderful everything is and how they are trying their best and that the questions will be answered soon. The government's definition of soon, unfortunately, does not correspond with what most of us think soon really means.
