subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to help alleviate the harsh and harmful effects on Canadian agriculture of its deliberate high interest rate policies, for its failure to honour its responsibilities to the Canadian agriculture industry during the present time of economic crisis, and for its failure to take other positive steps to assist the Canadian agriculture industry such as:
1)	extending the small business development bond to unincorporated farmers;
2)	amending the Farm Credit Corporation Act, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and the capital gains tax to ensure that Canadian farmers have access to necessary and sufficient funding; and
3)	redirecting its spending priorities to positive agricultural programs which would benefit Canadians as a whole.
He said: First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) home from his world travels. I hope the minister will stay in the chamber long enough, not only to participate in this debate but also to listen to some of the words of wisdom that I am sure will emanate from this side of the House. In any event, I say welcome back to our minister.
I think the motion we have just heard read is most appropriate in that it touches on and deals directly with a number of issues which are currently of tremendous importance to agriculture all across our nation. For that reason, I am pleased to lead off in this debate.
Over recent years, this House of Commons has not turned its attention to agriculture very often in an opposition day debate. Most of us would agree that it is important to turn our attention to this subject more often if we truly recognize the unquestioned importance of agriculture and the production of food to our nation. Our Canadian agricultural industry shares a disproportionately large amount of capital and operational costs when compared to most other industries. This is due mainly to the enormous amount of land required that at present day capitalized values, is completely impossible to justify in terms of agriculture production. Present day interest rates and escalating inflation are major contributors to this situation.
A recent feature story in The Globe and Mail pointed out that in Ontario debt service is now close to being the largest single farm cost. For 1980 it shows that cost to be $436 million, up from $374 million in 1979, an increase of 16.5 per cent in just one year. Feed costs in 1980 at $588 million were the highest. The story pointed out that by 1985, which is four years from now, Ontario farmers will owe $8 billion. It is fair to suggest that this same situation exists in most other farm areas across Canada.
In southern Alberta, one of our irrigation districts, irrigation farm costs have gone up this year by $6.14 an acre due to the
June 1, 1981

increased cost of natural gas alone. This is the natural gas used for fuel and manufacture of fertilizers. That is direct consequence of the two natural gas taxes, about which we are hearing so much in Bill C-57. It is tragic and most unfortunate but right across Canada we are now witnessing a very significant increase in farm bankruptcies and bank foreclosures, surely a discouraging situation for younger farmers and those who are about to start farming.
Since the Easter recess, we have been encouraged by public remarks of the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that he was truly aware of the extreme financial hardships in agriculture; that he was fully aware of the inequity and unfairness of present monetary and fiscal policies toward agriculture; and that he was most surely aware of the government's loan guarantees to the troubled Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson corporations.
The minister expressed support for the widespread and popular suggestion that the small business development bond should be modified and broadened in its application to agriculture. Surely there is a genuine need for this financing device to apply to unincorporated farmers and that its provisions include farm operating expenses as well as capital expenses.
After recent comments from the Governor of the Bank of Canada and from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), most of us have to conclude that this government has no plans other than to sit out the situation and follow the trend line of the United States Federal Reserve Board's interest rates. Yet in spite of this dismal outlook, there seems to be a feeling- indeed, it is the expectation of all sides in this House-that the small business development bond approach will be modified as so many members and agricultural groups have suggested. That is the very least the government can and should do.
I want to pause a moment to say that I am sure most of us have already noticed a letter from the Minister of Agriculture on this subject which appeared in today's Ottawa Citizen. 1 want to read into the record two short paragraphs so that we can all be conversant with it. In part, this letter reads:
Under consideration is a change to the small business development bond section of the act to allow unincorporated farmers and businessmen to qualify for up to $500,000 in low-interest loans.
That section restricts banks to interest charges of no more than 10 per cent.
I am also considering changing the lending policy of the Farm Credit Corporation by instituting a moratorium for three years on payments of interest and principal on corporation loans.
I was very glad to see that letter, and I hope there will be a follow up very shortly.
I want to come now to a subject which is a little closer to my heart, but nonetheless just as serious, namely the Canadian beef cattle industry. I have a few remarks to make about it. Our Canadian beef cattle industry is presently struggling with the economic situation that I outlined in my opening remarks which applies to agriculture as a whole. As cattle producers, we are seriously concerned about the future of our Canadian industry in both the short term and the long term. We suffer from a lack of confidence in the long-term future direction and development of our cattle industry.
Agriculture
In spite of a 2 per cent increase in beef-cow numbers in
1980,	according to a Statistics Canada figure, we are still probably at the bottom of the numbers cycle because of the fairly high rate of female slaughter in 1980. In my opinion, because of industry uncertainty we are essentially still at the bottom of both the breeding cycle and the beef supply cycle. Several other situations combine to add to our current cattle uncertainties.
Starting about a year ago, cattle feeders have consistently lost money for at last ten of the last 12 months due primarily to high interest rates, high corn and barley prices and abnormally high levels of live fat cattle imports from the United States over the last five months, a situation which still continues.
Another area of concern is the aftermath of three separate drought years across the western prairies in 1977, 1980 and
1981.	I hasten to point out that recent good rains, mostly in Alberta, have changed the current drought picture rather dramatically. However, there are still large areas in southern Saskatchewan that are still very dry and where grain and grass prospect are still very poor.
In spite of good rains, even in Alberta there remains a critical shortage of surface water because of winter drought over the last two successive winters resulting in no snow runoff water for both stock water and the many local, individual spring flood, forage feed projects. That is where the drought is hurting, even where we have had wonderful rains. There is no surface water because there was no snow for two years in a row. The significance here is that for the second year in a row forage feed supplies for cattle will be poor, and carried over reserves are almost non-existent after the previous severe winter for feed stocks.
Another significant drought development was the movement of an indeterminate number of feeder cattle to feedlots and cows with calves at foot to market this spring. There was a serious movement of this kind of cattle in both Alberta and Saskatchewan and maybe Manitoba, although I am not sure of that. In spite of our cattle industry's position at the bottom of the number and supply cycle, 1980 total meat supplies were at a record level of 218 pounds per capita, with beef and veal at a total of 90.9 pounds, pork at 71.3 pounds-an all-time high for pork-poultry at 51 pounds-also an all-time high-and lamb and mutton at 2.5 pounds per capita.
On April 15 the Minister of Agriculture announced there would be no stabilization payments for slaughter cattle sold in 1980. The announced 1980 support price was S75.88 and the national average market price was $76.37, just half a cent per pound above the support price.
In view of the state of the industry, as I just outlined, and the point that we are at in the cattle cycle, and in view of the potential proliferation of balkanizing provincial stabilization programs, discretionary pay-out for beef above the required minimum would have seemed appropriate by the minister this year. The minister has already established a precedent for

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
moving above the mandatory minimum support level of 90 per cent of the previous five-year average market price. He moved it up to 95 per cent and even to 100 per cent on other occasions. Why not this year when it is needed so desperately?
I now want to make some comments about the very recent hog stabilization payment announcement on May 21. Agriculture Canada announced a stabilization program of approximately $9, a few cents below it, per finished hog marketed during the fiscal year ending March 31. However, provincial hog stabilization payments will be subtracted from the amount payable under the federal plan. This is inconsistent with last year, when there were no penalties to discourage provincial subsidy programs and provinces now are actually being encouraged to get into some form of provincial subsidy. For example, Quebec has its own subsidy on weaner pigs and still gets the full federal payment while other provinces with subsidies at market hog level get no federal payment. Similarly, the British Columbia hog plan is not penalized because of the manner in which their program operates.
Over recent years the minister has been highly critical of the obvious balkanizing impact of the various provincial hog programs, and quite properly so. In this new announcement, not only is he inconsistent, but he is actually encouraging more balkanization of the Canadian hog industry. Moreover, many farmers, especially cattlemen, will now feel their concerns about stabilization are justified in that the government can manipulate the stabilization program in several ways, depending on the politics of the day and the money available.
Now some comments about the subject of beef imports. I am aware that the new meat import legislation will begin detailed examination in our standing committee tomorrow. I am very glad that we are getting to that stage of discussion; therefore, I do not intend to discuss that important bill in this opposition day debate. However, there are certain related matters pertaining to the guaranteed minimum access levels of beef imports that were negotiated during the Tokyo round of GATT negotiations that must be mentioned now.
I feel very strongly about the lack of incentive and confidence in the future of our Canadian cattle industry, as I have already indicated. This, referring to the GMA levels that came out of that Tokyo Round, is perhaps the single most important factor contributing to that negative and depressing feeling aobut our cattle industry.
It poses this key question: Is it worth while to spend 20 years or more becoming established in a beef cattle operation at the cow-calf-yearling level, on the grass, only to realize that our offshore competition will continue to get an ever-increasing share of our domestic beef market because of an overly generous guaranteed minimum access quantity base negotiated three years ago at the GATT, and that includes a human population growth factor to guarantee the growth of that offshore import share? That is the most depressing factor of all. It is discouraging cattlemen across Canada today. They are saying bluntly there is no future in beef cattle.
There is no question that our GMA level was set too high. This situation is more obvious now that our per capita beef
consumption is lower than when the negotiations took place. As a result of that human population growth factor, those offshore imports will make up a larger and ever-increasing share of our market relative to the U.S.A. since the United States did not agree to a similar human population growth factor in those negotiations.
I now come to another topic, which is very important to the cattle industry today because it addresses some of the serious concerns in which we are involved. I refer to it as a deferred income averaging trust proposal. The minister is well aware of this program. He has heard a lot about it in recent years.
Recently the Minister of Agriculture has been making suggestions with respect to some form of livestock, especially cattle, insurance program, probably to be patterned after the crop insurance program if that is possible, and I rather doubt it. A much more appropriate proposal is the concept of a deferred income averaging trust account that has been put together by some provincial governments and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, supported by a large number of its component members across Canada.
The plan is actually a form of personalized stabilization that would be applicable to any farmer. Essentially, the proposal would require changes in the Income Tax Act to allow individual farmers to set aside farm income into interest earning accounts in good years, for withdrawal as taxable income in low income years. Such accounts would be similar to RRSPs, but with a much higher ceiling. This personalized income averaging trust would deal directly with at least two inherent characteristics of agricultural production, especially in the cattle industry. They are not presently recognized and accommodated by our tax structure.
First, the cyclical nature of livestock production, especially beef cattle, results in quite dramatic changes in income. There are two aspects to this, the approximate ten-year duration of the cattle numbers cycle and the beef supply cycle, as well as the four-year individual production cycle of the cow-calf-yearling producer.
No other major agricultural commodity is subjected to such extremely long cycles, making planning, management and forecasting so difficult and even impossible. I made that statement several years ago and was challenged by an orchard man, a fellow raising apples. He told me how long it took to get an apple tree into production. That is probably true, but when talking about a major agricultural commodity I suggest that my remarks of the time still stand.
Weather and climatic conditions have a more profound and direct impact on agriculture than on most other enterprises, and I am sure that is an understatement. This climatic impact bears directly on net farm income whether localized or more general. Recent droughts-and I will cite three of them; 1977, 1980, and this year up to this stage-are good examples of this situation. Cattlemen learned long ago-I go back now to the lessons of the 1930s-that the prudent course to follow during a drought is to make your cattle numbers fit your available
June 1, 1981

grass and hay. This means cutting your cattle numbers sometimes very drastically. For the second year in a row I have had to do that very thing in my own operations.
An income-averaging trust would allow drought cattle sales, which would be well above normal because you would be selling off many more numbers in a given drought year, to be exempt from tax in that year. Surely it is illogical and without understanding for governments to tax disaster situations, but that is what has been happening under the present tax structure. We sell additional numbers of cattle in the face of a drought, the proper thing to do, and then have to face the consequences of a much higher taxable income.
Better pasture management would evolve and the income from such drought-induced forced sales would be left earning interest if we could use this income-averaging trust concept. That same income could be withdrawn in a subsequent low-tax year and used for restocking or for operating funds during a pasture and feed recovery stage. I would point out that that recovery stage of ranges that get eaten down to a point where cattle must be removed can sometimes take two, three or four years, before the grass comes back, assuming, of course, we have adequate rainfall.
With respect to additional supplies of forage hay needed for wintering the basic cow herd, I have always reasoned that, in the event of needed government assistance, such as in 1980 when the government brought in its herd maintenance program, the criteria should be based on the amount of such feed necessary over and above the long-term average requirements which are produced on the individual cattle unit.
This concept is based on the assumption that most cattle units have developed their own forage feed production systems over many, many years which would see them through two or three average winters. When one bad one comes along as a result of a drought, they would have their own reserves to carry them over. When that feed supply does not grow, this becomes another matter.
Our present tax laws work against these longer term cyclical, climatic and unpredictable aberrations I have already discussed. It is well known that farmers for years have attempted to defer and average their incomes through very destructive and wasteful year-end purchases of livestock, machinery and other production inputs. We are all familiar with that. In the month of December you size up your situation having regard to possible income tax and look at the merits of sometimes buying significantly large numbers of cattle or machinery. This is simply not good business but it becomes necessary under the present tax structure.
Let me hasten to add that the five-year tax averaging provision presently available to farmers is much less than adequate due to the extreme cyclical nature of the cattle industry. Many of our situations, as I already indicated, last much longer than five years.
1 suggest that the obvious merits of individual, self-managed stabilization accounts make this trust account proposal much less costly to the government and more efficient to administer
Agriculture
by the government. The proposal has the support of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and most provincial governments.
Before leaving this very important topic there is a related matter worthy of comment dealing with the Farm Credit Corporation. I am sure most of us are aware of the shortage of funds in the FCC. It has been an almost annual occurrence in recent years during the last quarter of the fiscal year. Most of us would quickly agree that additional funding is necessary, and necessary now, either from government or the private sector.
In this latter respect, why not use the individual averaging trust fund I have been talking about as a source of revolving funds for the Farm Credit Corporation? The FCC could administer the fund and it would be a continuing source of their financing needs. Among other advantages, the plan would be well received if only because of the concept of well established farmers helping young farmers get started, and that is a very necessary thing these days. I have never seen conditions more difficult for new farmers to get out on their own and get started.
Before concluding these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like briefly to assess the prospects and the challenges of the decade we are beginning, not only for agriculture generally but, perhaps more particularly, for our Canadian cattle industry.
First there is a developing challenge for Canada, especially western Canada, to help supply a growing beef deficit in the United States west coast market area. That deficit is presently
30,000	head of cattle per week, and that amount is about one and one half times Alberta's present production. This deficit in the U.S. west is presently supplied from the mid-west states which are considerably farther away from that market area than is the province of Alberta and most of the province of Saskatchewan.
With ever-increasing pressure on disposable income, consumers will be even more price conscious, especially of the more expensive foods, usually led by beef. All meats will become more competitive and consumers will be demanding a leaner grade of beef. This is, or will be especially true in the United States.
Rising production costs, such as fuel, fertilizer and much higher costs for transportation and distribution, will tend to keep cattle on improved forages longer, and cattle feeding and processing will tend to locate near the point of origin of those live cattle, and by that I mean, at least in Canada, in the black soil zones of the western provinces.
Our livestock transportation problems will worsen. Our railway stock cars are becoming obsolete very rapidly, and both railways have clearly indicated they have no intention of replacing them.
There is an urgent need for interprovincial truck licensing agreements to facilitate long-haul trucking.

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
The Crow rates and domestic feed grain pricing policies remain key deterrents to real progress in beef and pork production. The government should find ways of encouraging the two groups in the west, the western agricultural conference and the commodity coalition, to continue their negotiations which are now reasonably close to a compromise on this entire debate. I think some appropriate urging on the part of the government in its own way might help to bring this serious problem to a satisfactory conclusion.
Various provincial incentive programs in both cattle and hogs, some with top loading features, not only will eventually make federal harmonization more difficult but will impose an increasing risk of denial of access to United States markets for cattle and hogs. That is a very serious situation that could develop over the current decade.
Our Canadian meat market development plans must ensure that our quota allocation policies enable us to expand sales into the United States. Right now there are some factors working toward actually reducing those quotas, which is a situation we should never allow to happen because, after all, we are sitting next door to the biggest and highest beef market in the world and should take advantage of it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak to this motion today and I congratulate the member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for initiating this debate. I know him as a person who sincerely believes that the government must show concern for the farmer in these desperate times and must do something about high interest rates and the high debt load. I am also glad to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) here today. In my approach to this debate I am going to cover a lot of points besides that of cash flow.
I do have some difficulty in supporting some of the positions that the hon. member for Medicine Hat takes in many areas, although the first two points of his resolution could be adopted as a very helpful policy. We have heard much in this House and elsewhere about the sanctity of the family farm. All parties in this House agree on that. However, there the consensus seems to stop.
In order that food production can be maximized for Canada and the world we must give priority to the policy of security of farm income. Canadian farmers have always been eternal optimists, so much so that they continue to lose money year after year and still go on attempting to produce. Much of this optimism has been the result of minimal personnel requirements for running a farm and because those who work on the land are, in the best sense of the word, survivors. To survive, farmers have learned to make the most of as little as possible. The prairie farmer, and I speak mainly of grain farmers, for many years ran on what my father used to call haywire and horse manure. Haywire was used to repair almost everything, to keep the farm tied together. Horse manure was part of the basic fertilizer and kept the crops growing, and the horse was the main source of power.
In those days the farmer accepted whatever he got for his produce and very often received nothing for his labour. However, things have changed. Security costs more now. There is much more input into all types of farming these days from outside the farm, and most of these inputs must be purchased for cash. The farmer must have that cash to operate; therefore he must be paid enough for his produce to provide that cash. He needs that money to buy fuel, the price of which is going up daily; he needs it to buy power. A tractor nowadays can cost anywhere from $50,000 to $80,000. The cost of fertilizers and chemicals, which are closely related to fuel prices, are increasing very quickly. He has to have money to buy machinery and the increases in the prices of that machinery over the years has been fantastic. A machine costing somewhere around $500 before the war now costs $10,000, a twentyfold increase. The farmer needs to pay for labour, his own as well as others. Again, the cost has increased considerably. He also has to pay for transportation and for land.
Farming has survived as a way of life because many people find it so appealing that they continue to stay on under very adverse circumstances. But farming should be treated as any other business which must be nurtured and protected to survive. The family farm way of life has many natural enemies and the motion we are debating points many of them out. Surprisingly, the hon. member's motion and speech point out a number of suggested solutions. I say suprisingly because in his appeal he suggests that the government should intervene in farming more and more often. I am puzzled by that because what we have here is a free enterprise Conservative party asking the free enterprise Liberal party to intervene more often and more fully into the free enterprise area of farming. However, agriculture must have this kind of intervention to survive.
This crisis in farming that we are faced with right now is not new, nor is it unique. It is but another chapter in a 70-year period of instability of markets, fluctuation of prices and depression of incomes.
There are two basic problems facing agriculture today which must be considered. One is the cost of production and the second is the related question of prices, markets and incomes. The hon. member for Medicine Hat zeroed in on the problem of cash flow and the effect of the monetary policy of the government on the cash flow of farmers. The effects of the high interest rate policy and the monetarist policy on farmers have been greater than on most other industries. The government should not be asked at this time to deal only with problems of money. It should look at all the factors which are part of those two basic suggestions-the cost of production and the related question of prices, markets and incomes.
We need to establish as quickly as possible some kind of income security for farmers. I hope the minister agrees with this position. We can do this only by establishing producer control boards which have some effect on the supply of products on the market. We must prevent the dumping of agricul-
June 1, 1981

tural products on the Canadian domestic market. Some changes in the Meat Import Act will possibly start to control the dumping of agricultural products on the Canadian market.
Also we must establish market prices for all farm products at a level which will cover the cost of production. In the past this was part of the reason for the establishment of the board, but generally it should be a policy of the government right across the country. The farm is the only place where the free market is expected to work. One would not expect General Motors to produce cars by the thousands, put them on the market and then say, "How much can I get for them?" They start out knowing how much the cars will cost and add on a substantial profit; this becomes the price of the cars. However, farmers and other primary producers are forced to produce, put their products on the market, and hope they receive good prices for them.
Also we must establish some kind of insurance for that income, such as crop insurance, a stabilization policy or some type of insurance for all producers. We should look at some basic guaranteed income for farmers.
I should like to deal with the area of grain marketing because it brings into Canada a major portion of our foreign exchange. We must establish an initial price for grain going overseas or being sold domestically at a level which covers the cost of production. We must expand the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board so that all grains come under such a ruling. We should guarantee farmers some return on their grain, even in those years when the market is not large enough to handle the entire crop.
Now I would like to turn to the cost of production with which farmers must deal. In the last few years a major concern has been the cost of land. There is a myth that if farm sizes are increased, the total number of producers declines and the efficiency of farms increases; the larger the unit, the more efficient. If we compare a prairie farm of 2,000 acres which is being farmed by one farmer with two farms of 1,000 acres each, we will see which one produces the most grain. Size does not necessarily mean efficiency. The process of attempting to increase farm size has resulted in sharp competition and inflated prices. Therefore, we must do something about limiting the size of farms; this should be looked at as an area of concern.
We must prohibit foreign and corporate takeovers of farm lands, again to limit the size of farms and increase the possibility of family farms surviving. Also we must look at interest rates which allow farmers to buy.
The other day I was interested to hear the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) speak about the cross of gold which was being pressed upon Canadians. I think he referred to a speech of William Jennings Bryan who was running as the Democratic presidential candidate in the United States. At that time Mr. Bryan became the champion of the emerging west by saying that the west must be protected from eastern bankers and protection-minded Americans who wanted to retain the gold standard. Perhaps the hon. member for St. John's West is attempting to become the champion of the
Adjournment Motion
emerging west this time around. Mr. Bryan talked about the need for cheap money, the need for funds for farmers to break their land, equip their farms and harvest their crops. These are the same requirements which farmers have today.
We can all agree that the high interest rate policy of the government has the same effect now as it had back in 1896. I think the motion which is before the House should be accepted, since it condemns the government for not doing anything about this particular area of concern.
What we have seen in the past 30 months is the death of the cheap money policy for agriculture. This destruction by the Bank of Canada, conducted by Governor Bouey, aided by the hon. member for St. John's West when he was finance minister and by the hon. member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen), continues. Their policies may suit the bankers. They may be worth while as far as money and finance are concerned, but they do not suit the farmers in Canada today any more than they suited the farmers in the United States in Bryan's time, 1896.1 wonder what we can expect the Canadian farmer to do when he is faced with an interest and money policy which is based on beggar thy neighbour interest rates and which are designed to keep the balance of payments of the country at bay while farmers and other working people are offered a sacrificial lamb because of mortgage payments and the interest which they must pay. I also wonder what the farmers are supposed to make of the gradualism of the monetarist doctrine which is supposed to cut inflation while increasing everyone's interest costs substantially. If the government's policy is anti-inflationary, then thousands of Canadians have yet to find any evidence of it in their mortgage payments.
In addition to wanting the government's policy changed, as advocated by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, we want to put before this House the kind of policies which will change the structure of farming and agriculture in this country, to make it possible for a farmer to feel secure in his production.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with eagerness to the previous speakers to find some new suggestions which I had not heard before on how to overcome some of the problems facing agriculture today in Canada.
First, I would like to say to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) who led off the debate that he might have left the House with the impression-an impression which I am sure he did not wish to leave-that I was on a vacation travelling around the world. In order to be back here for this important debate today, I travelled steadily for 24 hours yesterday.
I also wish to say to him that I was not leaving a luxurious place but, rather, we were in a rather humble country called Yugoslavia, at the World Food Council meeting. I had discussions with the minister of agriculture there with regard to signing a memo of understanding to exchange scientists, technicians etc., between our two countries.
I was very eager to hear some new ideas, but I must say that I have not heard one so far. I hope the rest of the speakers in this debate from the party opposite will be more progressive, if you will pardon the pun, as time goes on.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat is very interested in the cattle business. He has been saying the same things about the cattle business for many years. He will probably say that I have been saying the same thing about it, too, for many years. We have known one another for quite some time.
The past ten years in the cattle industry has brought more change than in any 70 previous years of its history. I remember when I was First Minister of Agriculture my advisers told me that I could expect one bad year out of five. Then when we had two bad years they said they had never seen anything like it. Then when we had three bad years they said they had never seen anything like it and that something must be going wrong. They had not been taught the economics to show three bad years could happen out of five. Then when four years out of
five were bad in beef economy they did not know what to do because they had never been taught that kind of economics in school. It was something which they needed to develop a new theory about.
When we look at other areas of production we see some which are very healthy, regardless of what has been said by both hon. members who spoke before me. They left the impression that the whole of agriculture was economically unsatisfactory. They know that is not true. There are many sectors in agriculture today which are very healthy. For instance, the grain producing sector is pretty darned healthy when you look at the advance demand for payments which are interest-free.
By the way the two previous speakers spoke one would think there would be a tremendous demand for that money. This year those payments have been slightly more than the year before but less than SI00 million. I have said that we would use over $100 million in interest-free payments to farmers who could not deliver the grain, but the reason we did not have to give that money to them was because they were delivering their grain. The transportation system was handling that grain better than it ever did before. It handled a year and a quarter's supply of grain in 12 months, which is a phenomenal thing for that terrible, dilapidated transportation system which some people say we have.
Maybe we have some problems in our transportation system, but we still have the best one in the world, and that includes the United States of America. It includes the railroad transportation systems in Japan and West Germany where there are tremendous economic theories. You can read articles about what tremendous giants these countries are but their railroads have tremendous deficits every year. Those countries do not do very much about trying to overcome that deficit either.
When the hon. member for Medicine Hat talks about offshore beef affecting our markets, he is talking through his hat. That beef did not affect our markets at all last year-he knows that because they did not even fill their quota. We saw the largest depression ever in the price of beef last year. Why? Because there was overproduction of domestic red meats in Canada and North America which depressed the price of beef more than anyone imagined. There was unrestricted production of pork which took away from the beef market. Consumers swung over to the depressed prices of pork and discontinued eating beef. In turn, beef prices went down. That was the free market system working to its maximum, Mr. Speaker, causing hardship, heartache and economic disaster, the likes of which we have never seen before.
That system just does not work in 1981. The economic theory that the market will take care of its own needs is wrong and cruel. What I am saying, when I talk about supply management, is that other people have agreed with those kinds of measures. They are the people who are not writing me letters about going bankrupt and they number about 70 per cent of the producers in Canada. They are involved in provincial boards which provide marketing contracts. If they are efficient producers they produce high quality products and
June 1, 1981

receive a certain return, which is negotiated at the start of the year. The province the hon. member for Medicine Hat comes from has some of the strongest provincial marketing boards in all of Canada.
I do not understand why they do not want something better for beef, because under supply management one does not have the problems that he worries about, such as offshore beef or any other beef coming in from any other part of the world. Under GATT, the supply management type of system, imports are controlled that way. One does not have to worry. When beef took over 24 per cent of the market in Canada this year, was it for one week or for two weeks? No, it took over the slaughter market for more than nine weeks in Ontario, 24 per cent of it on average and 9 per cent all across Canada.
When I met the secretary of agriculture, Mr. Block, the other day, I said to him: "What would you do in your country if, say, we could take over your market that long?" He said: "Oh, you could not do it." He knows we cannot do it. We could ship all our cattle in Canada and only take over 10 per cent of his market for a few weeks, and he would never have to worry about us again. Then we would bring in all our meat from some place else in the world. We would do the same for coffee or anything else we do not produce: we pay according to the tune that the piper plays.
Coffee in Costa Rica costs $1 a pound, but we pay $4 for the same coffee in Canada because it is not produced here. We pay what the importers tell us that we will pay. I get so sick and tired of hearing about dreams that we are going to have this system work so good that everyone will be economically stable, prices will be stable, and economic conditions will improve.
However, when we see the other groups in Canada which are surviving, are doing a good job, are paying their bills and making investments, is there something wrong with that? If one reads the history of poultry production in this country, it used to be that a poultry producer was one of the worst risks that any bank, financial institution, or credit union could take on. Now when a poultry producer goes by, they wave and say: "Come on in; we have some stocks and securities that we want you to buy". The dairy farmers are not running around the block to get out of their way, nor are the poultry producers. Most of the horticultural producers in Canada are not doing that either. A strong agricultural economy has been built. The agricultural economy is very strong except for those two sectors which produce red meat, both pork and beef, because they are destroying one another as a result of overproduction, and hoping that the free market will solve their problems.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat said 1 was destroying the principles of stabilization in our country. The principles of stabilization are designed to provide equity among producers and equitable income in a fair manner. It says that in the act. A rich province might put in an expensive support program and then expect me to give it federal money, just as I do with a poor province which does not have the treasury to afford that
Agriculture
kind of system. That is not what the act says and that is not what it is for. It is to provide fairness. Read what the act says and you will have a better understanding.
Six years ago we proposed harmonization of stabilization to the provinces. Some of the farm organizations said: "No way, we do not want it." The provinces said: "Whelan and his government are wrong in providing that kind of organization", that kind of economic stability in agriculture. One of the provincial ministers was at the meeting. He went home and in six weeks implemented it in his province. The province was British Columbia, which is not a huge agricultural province. The federal government actually spends double the money in that province that the province does. However, he went home and put that plan into force for beef producers in British Columbia. Even some of the beef producers who objected to the income insurance plan joined it just as soon as it became law. I said to one: "Does it work?" He said, "You want to bet it works!" I said, "Does it cause inefficiency?" "You want to bet it doesn't cause inefficiency; it gives me an incentive to produce." It is the only province in the country which increased beef production when the rest went down. Some of them went slightly down, and some even went down more than that.
In different parts of Canada it is said they have such a tremendous program for beef in Quebec, they are going to take over the market for beef. They say they have increased production of beef in Quebec 100 per cent. A hundred per cent of what? It was hardly producing any beef before and it is hardly producing any now. It would take another 40 years at the rate it is increasing production, but it is guaranteeing 95 cents a hundred weight on the hoof for beef cattle. Is there something wrong with that program?
Let us make a comparison with rich Ontario alongside Quebec. Quebec spends $400 million plus on its agricultural economy. Rich Ontario, the largest agricultural province of all of Canada, produces 28 per cent of the agricultural worth of the whole nation, but spends only a measly $200 million for its agricultural schools and every other program. We spend more in Ontario than the province does. However, one would swear by what they are saying on the unfairness of hog stabilization, etc., that we are not doing anything for them. Did hon. members see what they did in eastern Ontario? The hon. member should be aware of that.

They received $11 million interest-free so they did not have to sell their crops in a distressed fashion. The hon. member knows that the industry in the province of British Columbia is probably in the healthiest state it ever has been in. Parts of that industry in Ontario have taken advantage of that same program.
Then we can move into the western grain stabilization program where we put in $2 for every $1 that the producers put in. How much did they pay out? They say we never did anything, but how much did we pay out? We paid out a total of about $360 million since that program has been in force. It was not totally federal money, but over two thirds was federal money which was paid out. That fund is building up rapidly because they did not have to make a payment last year. I doubt if they will have to make a payment this coming year either because there is a demand for grain and the prices will be good, as hon. members know. That is one of the reasons land is still as high priced as it is in western Canada. If the agricultural economy was so bad, would anyone pay a reasonable price, or even, some might say, an unreasonable price, for land?
The agricultural industry is healthy and can become even healthier with some of the things we need to do. These farmers should organize and run their own businesses. For instance, where are the most successful pork producers in the world? In Denmark. The distance from one end of Denmark to the other is equal to the distance between Toronto and Windsor. How many hogs are produced in Denmark? Twelve million hogs. How many hogs do we produce in Canada? With over 4,000 miles from sea to sea, we produce 12 million hogs. Who markets the hogs in Denmark? The farmers market 99 per cent of them. Who markets the hogs in Canada? Everyone does. There is a hodgepodge of marketing systems. The poor Americans are beings subsidized to the tune of some $30 a hog, yet it is one of the richest economies in the world. The same thing is being done for Japan. The same thing is being done for the people who send satellites around the earth and spaceships to the moon, the U.S.S.R. They are buying that product below the cost of production.
It is said that stabilization is the answer to the problem. The hon. member for Medicine Hat has heard me say that stabilization is not the answer, because I do not believe, if we run an efficient system, that we should have to use taxpayers' dollars to subsidize the United States of America, the rich economy of Japan or the U.S.S.R. in any fashion or form with such a high quality product. For instance, in Denmark the pork producers control the production of pork, how many sows, or hogs go to market, and so on. They run the processing plants and they run their world market selling system also. It is an efficient system.
Our pork producers are some of the most efficient in the world. They are not going broke because they are inefficient; it is because they become too productive. We hear economists and politicians say that the problem is that our society is not productive enough and that is why we have inflation. Do they mean that you have to be overproductive, that you have to go broke because you are so efficient in order for the economy to work properly? I say that is a cruel system, one that is unnecessary in the year 1981. It is time that some of the theories on those things were destroyed, just as some of our old farming techniques were many years ago.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) said that this day is a good thing. I say it is a bad thing, Mr. Speaker. The opposition has ten or 11 more of these days in June. If the opposition really wanted to do something they would give up five of them and we would bring in some legislation which could be passed through the House for the benefit of agriculture.

I want to say a couple of words about interest rates. I do not think any of us are happy about interest rates being 20 per cent and up, but I recognize that the issues are complex. Even if I were Governor of the Bank of Canada, I probably could not deliver 15 per cent interest rates tomorrow, as some of us would like to see. What I want to do is discuss the impact of high interest rates on agriculture and lay out for you my analysis of the current situation.
Interest rates are a significant cost of doing business for the farmer because the modern scale of agriculture requires a good deal of short, intermediate and long-term financing. Many people today do not realize that in a lot of cases $100,000 short-term credit is not enough; in some farm operations $200,000 is not enough. Some bankers are saying, "Sorry, old boy", or young man, or young lady, we are not going to let you have any short-term financing this year, even though you paid us $50,000", or $80,000, or $92,000, "in interest last year". Letters which I have received from farmers show how much they paid to the banks in interest last year, but some of the banks are saying that they will not go along with them this year. This is my main concern about high interest rates. The banks can do some of the things that members of this House have suggested within the act under which they operate. We
Agriculture
do not have to do what the House leader of the opposition suggested and bring in special legislation. They can provide longer-term money if they want to and they can give them moratoriums on their loans.
Some people try to put across the idea that the interest that banks charge is for handling the money. It is to cover the risk they take. Some people are under the impression that banks must have a dollar on deposit for every dollar they lend.
I have a letter from someone who has worked for one of the banking interests of this nation for many years. He said that in some instances they lend on a ratio of 100 to one. Imagine if I could sell eggs that way, Mr. Speaker! A farmer must have the produce but in many instances all the banks do is change paper. When interest rates increase suddenly and unexpectedly by almost one third as they did last December, and that high level is maintained over a period of months, there is the clear potential for an unacceptable degree of financial failure due to short-run cash flow problems. There has been a significant increase in the number of farm bankruptcies, and the situation bears close watching. I can assure you that the provincial ministers of agriculture and I are monitoring developments very closely.
It is my judgment that the problem at the present time is not serious enough to warrant the sweeping measures which are being proposed by some critics. It would be irresponsible to ignore the fact that realized net income of farmers is expected to be some 15 per cent to 20 per cent higher in 1981 than in 1980, even though interest charges are forecast to go up to 30 per cent.
It is obvious that while all farmers are paying higher interest charges, they are not all being forced to the wall as a result. For example, I am sure that if grain farmers in the west-I have already touched on this-had a hard run, more of them would have applied for interest-free advance loans.
The information I receive indicates that financial failure among farmers-and I am not just talking about bankruptcies- is concentrated among hog producers and beef feedlot operators, according to 90 per cent of the letters I receive. A market problem has clearly existed in these segments of the industry for some time.
I have explained to the hon. member for Medicine Hat that he is living in a dream world if he believes in the free market system where they move cattle across borders and across oceans. For instance, the cattle that came into this country and took over the slaughter market did not come by themselves. Some good corporate citizen of Canada bought them and brought them home and took over the Canadian slaughters market. He was able to make a few dollars on it and that is why he did it. That is the name of that game.
At that time I could have given interest-free money to farmers and they still would not have made a profit because those cattle depressed the market more than the money that would have been given to them interest-free. As the hon. member knows, the price of slaughter cattle dropped as much as 15 cents per pound as a result of the glut of big fat

American cattle that came here because they had no home to go to in the United States. Sooner or later I hope farmers in these segments of agriculture, pork and beef, will take to heart what I have been saying about the need for orderly marketing and better management of supply.
When high interest rates were added to the problems faced by hog producers and feedlot operators, who were basically in a loss position anyway, the inevitable exit of producers from the industry in a process of market adjustment was reinforced and made more painful. To say that high intererest rates have caused the farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and forced sales we have observed is to oversimplify the situation.
I took the initiative in April of requesting a meeting with The Canadian Bankers' Association. As a result of that meeting, the association agreed to convey to the top management of the chartered banks my view that, under present circumstances, the banks should be taking a more flexible and considered approach in dealing with farmers who are defaulting on their financial commitments. I am meeting with them again this week. The association also agreed to forward to the chartered banks, for reconsideration, cases of individual farmers which had come to my attention and which I thought deserved a second look.
My staff has been actively involved in talking to individual farmers and their bankers in an attempt to reach agreements that are satisfactory to both parties. In addition, the Farm Credit Corporation is giving special attention to hardship cases in which it is involved as a lender, either alone or jointly with the banks. To the extent that its resources permit, the Farm Credit Corporation is open to refinancing existing indebtedness when this promises to make the operation viable, and where it is necessary to make it viable.
I am not suggesting that this action on my part will put an end to bankruptcies and foreclosures among hog producers and feedlot operators. There are a lot of cases where there was a little equity in the operation to start with. The cumulation of losses in the last two or three years has produced a level of debt which would be unmanageable, and no matter how strong the recovery in the hog and cattle markets, it would be very difficult for them to recover.
However, I have no doubt that many of the farmers who are now defaulting on their financial commitments can have viable operations if they can just be tided over for a few more months, or even for two or three years, until markets turn around and they have time to readjust their operations. My message to the banks is that these farmers should be provided with the additional credit they need to carry on at a normal scale of operations for the next few months. My suggestion is that the banks should get away from the "rule-of-thumb" mentality that anyone who defaults is a bad credit risk and should not be given additional credit. Nor should the banks get too concerned about recent declines in the value of their security, associated with lower selling prices for hogs and cattle. When hog and cattle prices strengthen, it will not take
long for the value of the banks' security to climb back to earlier levels.
I am pleased to see indications that the top level managers of the chartered banks are already aware of the special nature of the problems facing hog and cattle farmers, in particular, and are taking a sympathetic and understanding approach to farm customers who are having difficulties. I think this is a case where the banks can do a great deal to help, simply by considering their long-run commercial interests and the special nature of the agricultural industry which gives them so much business.
Farmers last year paid out $1.5 billion in interest payments and this year they will pay out more like $2 billion. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that that figure is more than double the budget which the Minister of Agriculture has? My budget for all of Canada hardly reaches the $1 billion figure. We participate in all regions of Canada in support of agriculture. We do more in support of agriculture than do the provinces, something which a lot of people do not understand.
If hog and cattle markets do not develop in line with current projections, measures specifically directed at these segments of agriculture might be required to maintain the basic core of our productive capacity in these areas. It is a situation which requires close monitoring, and that is exactly what I will be doing.
In this context, I think it is important to keep the farm bankruptcy situation in perspective. There were 222 farm bankruptcies in 1980, up 77.6 per cent from the 1979 level. That is something which makes you angry when you hear that something has gone up 79 per cent; 79 per cent of what? It is just like beef production in the province of Quebec.
Our latest information indicates that there were 93 farm bankruptcies in Canada in the first four months of this year, up 40.9 per cent from the same period last year. If you check small business, you will see the phenomenal comparison. We talk about 222 farm bankruptcies, but nearly 7,000 small businesses went bankrupt at the same time. One has to bear in mind that the bankruptcy rate is less than one tenth of 1 per cent of the farmers in Canada.
A lot has been made of the fact that there never used to be bankruptcies to any extent among farmers. The fact that we now have a greater number of financial failures among farmers in part reflects the fact that farming is run more as a business now than used to be the case. More and more farmers are using borrowed money to finance expensive machinery and equipment and increasing outlays for fertilizer, top quality seed and other purchased inputs.

speechtext: My question is with regard to a figure which the minister mentioned. We on this side distinctly heard the figure 30 per cent mentioned with reference to an interest rate. Could the minister clarify that? I am sure we heard the figure 30 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I did use that terminology. I said some people are forecasting that interest rates could go that high. In fact, some economists are forecasting a 30 per cent interest rate.
In the World Food Council we discussed interest rates as they pertain to poorer countries, poorer than Canada; for instance, the Philippines. In some of the South American countries the interest rate is over 30 per cent at the present time. I don't know how countries can produce food under those circumstances. Some Canadian banking institutions are lending money in those areas. I am told that in some parts of Asia interest rates can be well over 50 per cent. We abhor that kind of thing.
I also pointed out that interest rates were not the only bad thing. For example, when you go to world price for energy the impact will be even worse than interest costs. Some people on the other side may be advocating higher energy costs, but people earn $1 a day in places like Tanzania where diesel fuel and gasoline cost $5 a gallon and eggs cost $2.50 a dozen. These are the things we see happening with the high cost of energy and the input costs of agriculture.
Let me tell members from Saskatchewan that the cost of potash has increased over 200 per cent. I know the potash corporation in Saskatchewan last year had an increase in profit of 150 per cent. I guess that is what you call social
Agriculture
democracy. That is the staff of life for many people. Potash fertilizer produces food. Economically millions of people in the world are being starved to death by interest, energy and fertilizer costs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for introducing this motion. I have to express my extreme disappointment with the minister because he did not address his mind to the main part of the motion, let alone to the remarks of the hon. member from Medicine Hat which included some very instructive comments and objective thoughts to help the farming community in this country who are faced, in the terms of the motion, with the "deliberate high interest rate policies" of this government. For the first three-quarters of the minister's speech we heard that we may not have increased beef production in Canada to service the American market, but we certainly increased the bull production in Canada which could have more than serviced the United States. A lot of the ministers remarks were not even relevant to the motion.
I like the minister. He is a genial fellow, but he has had his chance to speak. I have only 20 minutes, which is even less time than the minister, but I intend to say a few more relevant things, with respect.
The minister seems to thrive on appellations, but there is one which goes back to storybook fame. It is "Old Thunder". It is lots of noise, lots of thunder but no fire in the old system. This minister with his orations, diversions and camouflage in terms of real problems in the agriculture industry will be known as "Old Big Thunder" or "Soft Thunder". Like summer lightning, he has some flashes in the sky but does not produce any heat.
One of the reasons I am speaking today is because the farm community is faced with high interest rates. We are talking about the farmers of this land. We are not talking today about the small businessman and the pensioner caught in the inflationary spiral. We are not talking about the Denmark hog grower, who is not suffering from 22 and 24 per cent interest rates. We are talking about Canadians.
The minister criticized the hon. member for Medicine Hat by saying: "Oh, well, you always say the same old thing." Of course the farmer, the small businessman and Canadian citizens always say the same old thing. This minister should come down from the clouds and get back into the fields of Canada and deal with Canadians. He will find that the farmer in the east, in the west and in Ontario, where bankruptcy is high, is saying the same old thing, that 23 per cent interest on loans for short-term capital is too high to be able to run a productive farm.
The rate of bankruptcies, which were not even heard of in earlier days, is now very high. As the minister said, last year 222 farms went out of production and already in the first quarter of this year there were 93. Those are farms that are

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
out of production and will not come back into production for some time.
In Nova Scotia there is a farm loan board which provides substantial short-term help to farmers caught in this squeeze. Therefore, we do not have at the present time this horrendous bankruptcy situation. In Ontario, which used to be the heartland of Canada, I know of two cases where the farmers just walked off the land. They could not afford to pay 22 per cent on short-term money. They could not do what the hon. member for Medicine Hat suggested in terms of reducing in an immediate way farm credit procedures in order to get short-term help.
Of course people are saying the same old thing. They will continue to say the same old thing as long as this government sits on its derriere and tries to camouflage the fact that the farm community is faced with insurmountable problems as a result of interest rates that have never been so high.
I have no sympathy for the minister today, who outside the House is a genial fellow. I have no sympathy for the fact that he had to fly for 24 hours in order to get back here to participate in this debate. If the debate has done nothing else, it has at least brought the minister back to Canada to talk about Canadian problems and deal with the thoroughly irate farming community from coast to coast.
The Toronto Star, that pillar of journalism which is the masthead of the Liberal party, says day in and day out that the interest rate policy of this government is folly. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has asked for short-term help to the tune of $200 million to assist farmers to renegotiate loans or who are caught in a mortgage vise. They want help now, not down the road.
We cannot accept the policy of gradualism of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). It will lead us right into the financial sink and down the tube if we follow that minister who does not bring in any policy. The Minister of Agriculture is monitoring the problems. All you have to do is look at the farm digest and farm papers to know that the farm community is in dire straits. Obviously some parts are stronger and healthier than others.
This minister comes back, moans and groans, rubs his tired eyes and talks about the sacrifice he made by travelling 24 hours to be here in the House of Commons to talk about something that is basic and important to every Canadian from coast to coast. That is the problem of the farm community having the productive capacity to produce food for all Canadians. Instead of talking about our potential to expand, all we received from him this afternoon was claptrap.
Every farmer in this country has sacrificed more than the Minister of Agriculture in trying to meet unconscionable interest rates. I hope they were watching television today to see the Minister of Agriculture try and camouflage the real problems. He did not even address the motion of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. It is not a highly provocative, partisan motion.
The speech by the hon. member for Medicine Hat was most even and objective. That member, a past president of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, is one of the most respected members of the farm community of this country and was so long before he became a member. We are thankful he is now a member so that he can bring to the floor of this House some of the concerns of the farm community, let alone his special knowledge and interest in the cattlemen of this country. I am glad the minister was in this House to hear some of the hon. member's positive proposals. However, the minister did not even address them. The motion reads:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to help alleviate the harsh and harmful effects on Canadian agriculture of its deliberate high interest rate policies, for its failure to honour its responsibilities to the Canadian agriculture industry during the present time of economic crisis, and for its failure to take other positive steps to assist the Canadian agriculture industry such as:
1)	extending the small business development bond to unincorporated farmers;-
The hon. member for Medicine Hat referred to a letter in the paper which indicates that the minister may be moving after he monitors a little more. The motion continues:
2)	amending the Farm Credit Corporation Act, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and the capital gains tax to ensure that Canadian farmers have access to necessary and sufficient funding; and
3)	redirecting its spending priorities to positive agricultural programs which would benefit Canadians as a whole.
That is a fairly even motion in view of the crisis facing Canadian agriculture today. The Science Council of Canada stated that if we develop our potential in agriculture, we can double our production by the year 2000. We must redirect some of our interests, energies and priorities into the farming community. However, all we got today was the same old camouflage evasion from "Old Thunder", except for the very last part of his speech.
I am glad the hon. member for Medicine Hat asked about the 30 per cent interest rate. From listening to the minister, 1 thought he was relating to what people were saying was going to happen in Canada, not in the Philippines or Chile. In any event, the minister clarified that in part. Let us hope there will be no more talk about 30 per cent interest rates. The 20 and 22 per cent interest rates are too high for the farmer to pay.
The minister complained that we are saying the same old thing. Interest rates have been going up on a monthly basis with a few little blimps downward every so often. However, the farmer is locked into a year contract or demand note, and a longer contract if it is a mortgage. Co-ops do not change that quickly. The farmer cannot readjust his planning to conform with these unconscionable interest rates. That is the fundamental problem affecting the farm community across the country.
I was going to compliment the minister before I listened to his oration. There are areas where we can move very positively in agriculture and where we can redirect expenditure and produce more. The hon. member for Medicine Hat talked about an averaging indexing proposal. The minister did not reply to that. It seemed sensible and logical. In good years the farmers could salt some away and use it in poor years. Because
June 1, 1981

the minister did not reply to that, I am a little hesitant to compliment him.
Two weeks from today the minister and I will be at the official opening of the research station at Kentville, in Annapolis Valley in my constituency. That agricultural research station is for all of Atlantic Canada. There is no area of agriculture in this country where there is more potential than in research and development. 1 am certainly glad that we are going finally to have the official opening of this research station.
I could cite chapter and verse some of the problems there are now. I am sure the minister is aware of them. Unless we plan now for the future, some of the smaller markets in terms of dollars will be lost to Atlantic Canada. We are not like the big people from the west and we do not have the wealth of Ontario. Our low-bush blueberries in Atlantic Canada account for something like $18 million to a lot of farmers who need that income, yet right now, because of developments in high-bush blueberries in Michigan, New Jersey and the Carolinas in the United States, we in Canada are becoming very uncompetitive. Unless research is done now in terms of more mechanical means of harvesting blueberries to cut down on high labour costs and in terms of pruning these bushes rather than burning them with high cost oil and things like that, we will lose these specific benefits in Atlantic Canada from this industry. Obviously, they are very small, at the start, but when you count up all those blueberries and you find you lose $18 million, you realize that this is something very valuable to many farmers in Atlantic Canada.
I see that my time is almost up, but I was bothered by the minister's remarks today. I would have respected him even more had he come in and said he knows there are a heck of a lot of problems in the agricultural industry. Anyone who is confronted with these interest rates, whether he is a businessman or a millionaire, particularly farmers with crops that have to be planned on a seasonal basis, is obviously facing tough times.
I compliment the hon. member for Medicine Hat for bringing forward this motion. Those are my points about the small business development bond program and some of the proposals by the hon. member. I would really have appreciated the minister giving a considered reply to the speech by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, or at least responded to his motion, rather than giving us utter garbage for the first three quarters of his speech.
The minister knows more about this industry than his remarks indicate. From time to time I believe he really does have a sincere interest in agriculture. But I think my appellation of "Old Thunder", "Big Thunder", or whatever you want, is unfortunately too accurate. While the minister may have, and does have when he is not so tired, a sincere interest in agriculture, I am afraid that often the sound he makes in cabinet does not provide results. That is certainly the case with the sound he makes outside, but how much weight he carries in
Agriculture
cabinet councils I am not sure. With his interest in agriculture he knows better than I that more research and development with a shift into higher spending has to be accomplished if we in Canada are to stay competitive in many areas.
There are many problems facing agriculture now in Atlantic Canada. Somebody earlier referred to GATT. Let me talk about research and development. We are at a lower level in Canada in terms of research and development than the United States and Russia. I have read several interesting articles on this subject and I intended to quote from one at quite some length. The agricultural reporter from Alberta, Mr. Schmidt, reports in a very interesting way on the comparison between the United States, Canada and Russia in terms of expenditures for research and development. Canada is at the bottom of the list. I understand that the minister's officials and Science Canada suggest that a dollar spent on research will in effect produce $7 in return.
I know the minister has been pretty busy and may not have had a chance to digest the traditional annual brief from the Agricultural Institute of Canada, but I hope his officials have considered it. It was presented to all the party caucuses in the Parliament of Canada, the government, Conservatives and the NDP. On page 1 of the brief there is a most interesting section on research and development which shows, in effect, the returns you get when you really spend money on research and development. Some of these facts apply very much in my riding because of the enhancement and development of the broiler industry. On page 2 of the brief, among other things, appears the following:
The benefits accruing from agricultural research have been well documented. The safeguarding of wheat from the ravages of rust provided a benefit to cost ratio of 482:1; research leading to the reduction of fallow acreage in Manitoba provided a benefit to cost ratio of 278:1 but the benefit should continue to accrue for decades ahead; a benefit to cost ratio of 260:1 was estimated for R and D on chicken broilers; in Ontario input cost of $32 million for the improvement of corn provided additional returns of $2.6 billion or an investment return of 80:1.
I think my time has just about run out, but the second short paragraph on this page shows the Canadian picture in relation to that of the United States. It states:
Ten years ago (1970), the Canada Department of Agriculture expenditure was 3.7 per cent of total Canadian Government expenditure. By 1978, agriculture expenditure had dropped to 2.4 per cent of total government expenditure and in 1979, agriculture expenditure was reduced still further to only 1.9 per cent of total government expenditure. Of this, only 10.9 per cent was expended on agricultural research.
There were many proposals and positive recommendations, many of which have been made before. Frankly, I think Socrates said a long time ago that there has not been a new philosophic or perhaps agricultural thought that has never been advanced before by man. These ideas are framed in different ways. A lot of these things have been said before. There is a problem in terms of research and development. Anyone can play with figures, including politicians, farmers and certainly financiers. If we are to plan for the future and look down the road ten years-and it often takes that long to do the work and see the results-instead of a declining budget for research and development within the agricultural budget we must have lead money and lead time. We must have a

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
surplus of funds for research and development in agriculture. If we are to have the same budget, let alone a declining budget, the inflationary factor will mean we will be spending all the money and time on research and development just to maintain the status quo or to plug the holes in the proverbial dike wall of research and development, with no plans for new holes in that wall down the road. We must spend more money in order to develop better apple, potato, wheat, soft wheat and hard wheat crops, you name it, to say nothing of the low-bush blueberry crop that must be competitive so we do not lose our markets.
I do not want to trespass on time as I know other hon. members want to speak. We should perhaps have two days' debate on this subject, one for western agriculture and one for eastern agriculture. There are very real problems and I know the minister is aware of these. I certainly hope his officials are aware of problems in relation to the GATT negotiations and the potentially adverse effects of valuation procedures and freight rates in border states. If we are not careful we may be in greater difficulty because of valuation procedures and freight rates for imports. Valuation is supposed to be neutral and freight rates are supposed to be taken into account, but in terms of Canadian markets and producing areas adjacent to border states we could find ourselves in the position of having a real flood of imports.
There are many things one could talk about in the field of agriculture. 1 could even refer to the veterinary college in Atlantic Canada, the matter of feed grains in eastern Canada, the effect of marketing boards on price stability and production, and interest rates to consumers. There is so much to be said about agriculture, but I think the bottom line of my concluding remarks about agriculture is that I just wish that "Old Big Thunder" would not thunder so much from time to time-
