subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to comment very briefly on today's opposition motion concerning interest rates. Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speeches of two opposition members, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) and the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), but neither of them came up with constructive suggestions. They criticized the 10 per cent segment of agriculture which may be in the doldrums, but they forgot to point out that 90 per cent of Canada's agricultural community is operating at full capacity.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that Agriculture Canada and the minister are aware of the problems caused by recent hikes in interest rates, particularly to young farmers who are just starting out in the agricultural business and to a few specialized producers involved in hog and beef production. Naturally,
one cannot remain indifferent in the face of bankruptcy reports, as the minister said earlier, because in certain areas the bankruptcy rate is as much as 70 per cent higher than at the same time last year. Still, although interest rates do create serious problems for all farmers, the number of bankruptcies in Canada has always been very low. As I recall, a few moments ago the minister gave us a few statistics to show that last year 222 farm operations went bankrupt as compared with over 7,000 small businesses. Of course there are fewer bankruptcies in agriculture than in any other field. However, in most instances we are not in a position to find on our own the corrective measures to problems whose scope extends far beyond the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture. In the field which concerns us, namely assistance to farmers, the existing programs coupled with certain measures which have already been taken by our department contribute to lighten the farmers' financial plight.
Last week, when regional development deputy minister Couillard appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I heard opposition members belittling the new reorganization in the Department of Agriculture. And yet that reorganization was carried out to meet the needs of farmers and enable them to improve their efficiency and their productivity. It follows that when they raise their productivity they can lower their production costs. Throughout the debate, during an hour and a half last week, they harassed the deputy minister before the Standing Committee on Agriculture, telling him they did not understand why the Department of Agriculture has made changes within that service. Yet it was quite simple, and today members opposite blame the Department of Agriculture for doing nothing. It was precisely measures like those taken by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion that allow farmers to improve their production.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, as a result of recent increases, interest rates of chartered banks in Canada have reached almost 20 per cent. While everybody is clearly affected by those increases, farmers are especially hard hit, because they need short-term and long-term loans to purchase inputs such as the machinery, the seed, the fertilizers, etc. required for their annual production and to improve their operations. A while ago, the Minister of Agriculture pointed out rightly that some products such as chemical fertilizers from Alberta had increased by 200 per cent, that potash products had substantially increased. We did not hear the members opposite, especially those from Alberta, refer to such increases. Pork producers, of course, like all those whose prices are not controlled by marketing boards, are especially affected by rising interest rates. If we compare them with dairy producers who have a National Marketing Board, quotas throughtout the country and indexed increases for industrial milk and fluid milk.
In my own constituency of St. Hyacinthe, there are a lot of farmers in just about every type of production. I can assure you that the dairy producers are not complaining because they
June 1, 1981

come under a marketing board. There are of course many farmers in my region who are pork producers. Since there was no pork marketing board until quite recently, when the Quebec producers voted for a board about four to six weeks ago, these producers have known fluctuating prices and they have certainly overproduced, which has brought about a fall in prices. Of course, decreasing prices and increasing interest rates do not help this industry. Not only must the farmers obtain bank loans at rates between 18 and 20 per cent to maintain costly operations and improve their buildings and equipment, but market prices are too low to allow them to get a sufficient income from their product. As I have just explained, Mr. Speaker, marketing boards make all the difference.
It is a known fact that, at the present time, financing costs represent approximately 15 per cent and can even reach up to 30 per cent of operating costs. However, the situation is perhaps of greater concern for young farmers and new operators who have to bear the costs of big mortgages in addition to the burden of those costly productions. These young farmers who want to make a start on our Canadian farms are the backbone of our farming sector and they are often forced to give up without any hope of being able to reintegrate the farming sector on the short term. We know, Mr. Speaker, that a disproportionate number of pork producers are now defaulting on their farm loans. The minister met recently with the Association of Bankers. We shall be meeting the association again this week.
I have personally met several bankers in Quebec. We are simply asking them to be a bit more indulgent toward hog producers. Several small processors also have problems because they have to support very large stocks from one crop to the next at current interest rates. Last year, farmers paid $1.5 billion in interests, and this figure will probably reach $2 billion this year. I am speaking about what action we intend to take, I have just mentioned that there have been meetings with The Canadian Bankers' Association. The Minister met them at the end of April and we shall be meeting them again this week. The Minister has pointed out that the banks and the government have a shared responsibility to consider the long-term interests of Canadian agriculture and our society as a whole during economically difficult periods.
The Minister has asked the bankers to consider refinancing agricultural loans now due over a longer period. I believe that it would be physically possible for the banks to do so to help the farmers who are now going through a difficult period, like all the other industrial sectors. As a result of this meeting, the association agreed to recommend a more flexible policy for the management of agricultural loans to its members, to the bank branches, in view of the high interest rates. The association has agreed to discuss with its members the possibility of paying particular attention to those who are facing real problems, such as pork and beef producers. The farmers have just completed their sowing, and they have had to invest large amounts of money in fertilizers and seeds. And considering the current low prices in the pork industry, it is my feeling and my
Agriculture
conviction that the banking system will act on the request made by the minister just recently.
Of course, borrowers from the Farm Credit Corporation pay much lower interest rates than other borrowers. On April 1, 1981, the rate was set at 14 per cent. I would like to point out to opposition members that this is only 2 per cent more than last year, when they were the government, and this indeed was more than a year ago because they had raised the Farm Credit Corporation's rate to 12 per cent. And since that time, we have raised it to 14 per cent, which is only 2 per cent more charged on loans from that corporation.
The flexible repayment facilities offered by the Corporation are based on the nature of the borrowers' farm production and last year, when pork producers faced difficulties, each case received special attention and was dealt with fairly. There have been time extensions to repay farm loans. Four thousand Five hundred long-term loans were granted in 1980-1981. Currently, the government is seeking as a priority a way of making more funds available to the corporation. As stated earlier by the minister, if the various pieces of legislation on the Order Paper can proceed-and there are now five or six in the name of the Minister of Agriculture-we will be in a position, hopefully within a reasonable time frame, to amend the Farm Credit Corporation Act so that farmers may obtain bigger loans. It must be kept in mind that both in Ontario and in Quebec farmland worth $500 per acre hardly 15 years ago is now worth $1,500 and $2,000 per acre. And as far as I am concerned, I can say that the family farm, my father's 100 acres, was sold for $1,500 an acre in 1960, and on resale just a month ago, it brought $2,000 an acre, which clearly shows the high increase in farm prices. What this means, Mr. Speaker, is that although the farmer must face high increases in interest rates like all other industries, his farm property has increased in value. The example I have just given is very typical.
' Farm improvement loans granted between January 1, 1980, and March 31, 1981, totalled over $49 million. The maximum interest rate charged cannot exceed the chartered bank prime rate by more than 1 per cent. In addition, over the weekend I met people involved in the selling of farm equipment, seed grain and other input supplies. All of them told me that in recent months they have had at least a 20 to 25 per cent increase in sales. In connection with the hog stabilization program which is intended to help producers, the minister recently announced stabilization payments of $8.96 per head marketed between April 1, 1980, and March 31, 1981. This means that the total cost of the program could reach or even exceed $100 million. That, Mr. Speaker, is yet another move by the Department of Agriculture and the Canadian government to help out the farmers in Canada. I can say that in the province of Quebec which accounts for 38 to 40 per cent of all of Canada's hog production, approximately $40 million will be spent to help Quebec hog producers.
There have also been improvements with a view to processing applications more quickly and we have so advised the

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
organizations with whom we have met recently. I was accompanied by a group of hon. members at that meeting with representatives of the UPA, the Cooperative federee and the Association des meuniers. We promised them that all correctly filled forms would be given special attention and that within four to five weeks of their being received farmers, precisely because of those high rates of interest, would receive their hog stabilization payments. The Agricultural Stabilization Board and the Department of Agriculture have introduced these stabilization payments in order to provide Canadian producers with fair and average support and income.
Agriculture Canada and the federal government have established many other programs designed to help producers increase their production and avoid disaster in periods of hardships such as the one we are now experiencing. For instance, there are the research programs. Over $155 million of the over-all departmental budget have been earmarked for research. In the riding represented by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) a new research centre is soon to be opened. Earlier, the hon. member spoke of Canada's fourth veterinary college. One has to understand the reasons why this college is not yet under construction. There are four provinces each striving to get it. Once they are agreed about a site, Agriculture Canada will assuredly abide by the recommendations of the Howell report submitted over two years ago.
The crop insurance program is a cost-sharing program where federal and provincial governments each contribute 50 per cent. The bill setting up Canagrex, an agency specifically entrusted with exploring for new markets, will soon be introduced and will hopefully be supported by the opposition. Only last week, I replied to a question put by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Caron) concerning maple syrup overproduction in that area. It is in instances such as these, Mr. Speaker, that Canagrex, which is to be responsible to the Department of Agriculture, will be involved in finding new offshore markets. This could work for maple syrup as well as pork, eggs, chicken, beef, or cheese. We know that Canadian producers are increasing their production considerably each year, which means that there is overproduction in many areas. As far as food supplies are concerned Canada is definitely not an importing but an exporting country. We need an agency like Canagrex, which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) wants to set up, to help our producers.
We also have programs for drought-stricken ranchers. I would say that Agriculture Canada did everything possible last summer to help those western farmers who were severely affected by the drought. As far as stabilization payments are concerned, I just referred to them in connection with hog producers. We have had them for hog and potato producers and we will probably have them for apple growers. The Agricultural Stabilization Act provides for nine areas of production where, whenever the market price does not match production costs the Agricultural Stabilization Board steps in, which means of course the Department of Agriculture. As the Minister of Agriculture mentioned earlier, over $3 million
were paid out to Canadian producers since the legislation was enacted.
Bill C-46, to regulate the importation of meat, that the Standing Committee on Agriculture will start considering tomorrow, is another major piece of legislation designed to help Canadian farmers. I hope members opposite will make sure it is adopted without delay. Bills C-32 and C-33 as well as several other bills now on the order paper are all pieces of legislation put forward by Agriculture Canada and the Canadian government to improve farm products. I should like to deal now with the Feed Freight Assistance Program of the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. When the chairman of the Canadian Livestock Feed Board appeared before the standing committee a few weeks ago, members of the opposition dared say to him: "You should call it the Eastern Canada Livestock Feed Board."
It is not with such remarks that we are going to help our farmers, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that our hon. friends should reconsider their position from time to time. To conclude, Mr. Speaker, we do not intend to take extraordinary steps just now. Our agricultural industry is sound and the changes already made to existing programs should adequately help Canadian farmers through this critical period. This situation is very likely to be temporary; should it persist, however, we would then consider more drastic measures. We deplore the problems now facing Canadian farmers, but we feel that we should not be the only ones to help them. The provincial governments should do their share too. Agriculture Canada is aware of its responsibilities and we intend to prove it.

Mr. Speaker, I think one of the most frustrating situations is to have to sit and listen to a member such as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) discuss some of the government's measures in a relatively nonchalant-I will not say an uncaring-way, an unfeeling way for a whole sector of our economy, which is in a great deal of difficulty right now. Indeed, it is in a crisis situation today.
Before the parliamentary secretary leaves I would like to address a specific point which he mentioned. I think the frustration I feel must be shared by the agricultural community across this country. I know that he will agree with me when I say that there is a large segment of the agricultural economy right now which is in big trouble-if he will admit that. One thing which must happen is that there must be a federal-provincial understanding of the problem. He is proud of the record he has. He says that it is the provincial governments which must come to the assistance of the farmers. The provincial government of Ontario came to the assistance of the hog producers just last week with a $10 million subsidy. Do you know what the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) did? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner adjournment I was trying to identify one of the major difficulties of the government in dealing with this problem. The simple fact is that there is a lack of understanding of the difficulties involved in the basic farm production unit simply because research, the complete orientation toward marketing and the whole agribusiness are devoted to looking at international events and at things which are happening in other countries. At the same time, we do not have in place any specific way of determining what is happening to an individual farm unit.
I certainly hope that as we start this debate again, the fact that there are so few hon. members present on the opposite side is no indication of the sincerity of the government on this issue. I think that the few who are now present are really part of the problem. We will not resolve the difficulty until they start to face the situation and appreciate that it is truly a crisis, not something which is going to go away as long as they do not react too strongly in one way or another. 1 want to assure them that this is a real crisis. The situation is very real. At the local level, the basic farm unit, particularly the beef and pork production sectors, is in severe difficulty today.
If we look back a little, we find that in 1941 there where 3.2 million farmers in this country. That is an indication of what is happening in the agricultural sector. There has been a gradual decrease in the number of farmers. Each year in Ontario alone there are 1,000 fewer farmers. This will result in a reduction of the basic farm unit. Even though individual farms are becoming more productive, we are seeing the concentration of the agribusiness in the hands of fewer and fewer, to a point where I think we must decide whether we are going to maintain this very economical and important basic unit which has given Canada what is really a very cheap source of food. Unless attention is paid to that factor, we are all going to suffer significantly in the end.
Another point that I would like to make is that these are people who are probably friends and neighbours of some of the hon. members opposite, people who probably voted for their party as well as ours, and people who may have even voted for the NDP party. However, the fact is that all of these people
now find themselves in situations similar to the farmer who spoke to me yesterday for about an hour. He had been in the business for ten to 12 years, had built up his whole herd and put together a farming operation including machinery and significant land holdings. He came to a situation where he had to sell his basic farm unit to a foreign buyer. He must now find some way of recovering his financial losses and regaining a sound economic basis. He was a good manager. This is a farmer who knew the business, who had grown up on a farm and who understood agriculture. Through no fault of his own, he had to accept the prices which were being offered for his commodity over the past two or three years. Eventually he found himself in a position where he had to decrease his total production significantly. Lately this has happened to many people.
A number of things have taken place. One of the most significant groups to offer proposals for solving the problem is the Canadian Cattlemen's Association which has identified the difficulties in the beef sector. It has mentioned high interest rate costs, the inflationary increases in a lot of farm input costs, high energy costs, the importation of live fat cattle from the United States, and the difficulties experienced in 1976 when there was no import law. All of these things are balanced by the fact that farmers still have to accept poor prices for their commodity at the farm gate. They cannot see any way of recovering those losses in the reasonably near future. A number of factors are involved in that but I shall not dwell on them now.
What this amounts to in concrete terms is that in my constituency alone, the area of Bruce-Grey, this year the cost to beef producers will be $20 million. That represents the subsidy that those farmers are giving to the consumers of Canada. It is the cost to that one segment of the agricultural industry, and I think that is going to spell gloom for the whole industry, particularly in Ontario.
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture has made some specific proposals regarding interest rates and in conjunction with these, the Conservative party has made several significant proposals as well. These have been put before the House on other occasions and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture is aware of them. They deal with things like the Farm Credit Corporation and the possibility of increasing its funding by perhaps $150 million or perhaps reconsidering the interest rate it is charging now of 14 per cent instead of the 10 per cent it was years ago.
We are also considering whether the Farm Credit Corporation would be able to provide access to funds from regular banking or lending institutions which could be of more advantage to the farming industry. In addition, we are examining the stabilization program to see if improvements can be made to it so that the return to the farmer could be increased to the point of enabling him to survive. We are also examining relationships between the federal and provincial governments. Some provincial governments have offered to set up review


June 1, 1981

agencies to deal with farmers who are in distress. Perhaps a mechanism could be set up to review specific cases of farmers in trouble and to find ways to assist them. This would be a valuable contribution by both the federal and provincial governments.
At the moment there is an offer from this side of the House, which I believe has the support of the New Democratic Party, regarding the small business development bond. In this House this afternoon we heard the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) speak about a program to let people know what the bond is all about. That is fine, but perhaps it should have been done a year ago. What we need now is an improvement in this bonding mechanism so that it can be used by unincorporated small businesses and farmers for operating capital and inventory. Perhaps it could be extended beyond this year. Those things could be done now and we on this side have offered to have a one-day extended debate. I think the government should accept the offer.
In 1980 the Minister of Agriculture promised that he would do something for the farming community, but that promise has not been kept. I think that the will to do something is there, on the part of some hon. members opposite at least. Unless action is taken now, we know that by the fall of this year the number of farmers in trouble will not just have doubled or tripled but will have increased by five or ten times. There will be an increasing number of farms for sale and the entire agricultural economy will be on the verge of collapse. In the end, not only the farmers but consumers will suffer because of the lack of a constant and secure source of reasonably priced food.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a few moments tonight on the role of agricultural research in the Canadian economy. The attainment of the present success of the Canadian agrifood sector, developed under many natural disadvantages, has depended upon an expanding base of research and technology. The Canadian agrifood system is, I suggest, basically sound both technically and economically. During the post-war period productivity increased to almost double that of the other non-agricultural sectors. The system provides more than the equivalent of Canadian food requirements, and export sales amounted to about $8.0 billion in 1980 plus $95.0 million worth of food which was made available to the world food program. The system supplies Canadian consumers with adequate, high quality food at a cost of 17.8 per cent of consumers' disposable incomes, which is close to the lowest percentage of any country in the world.
Agriculture Canada, under the leadership of this government, has continued to develop strong mission-oriented, agricultural research and development programs which are making important contributions to crop and livestock improvement, to the efficient utilization of Canada's agricultural resources, and to market development. Such programs are accomplished through close federal-provincial co-operation, particularly in technology transfer, and are committed to the following specific areas of research and development.
Agriculture
Basic research is a prerequisite to achieving advances. Our programs in a number of promising areas, such as nitrogen fixation, genetic engineering, somatic hybridization, and cryo-preservation are progressing and have provided some interesting practical results. The opportunities offered by biotechnology and especially its impact on the food processing industry, are currently being investigated.
Because of climatic and soil limitations, the improvement of crop production is particularly critical in Canada and a number of major programs are committed to this effort. Hardier varieties, better adapted to short, cool seasons, higher yielding capacity and of better quality are being produced. Resistance to crop pests is also important. This year alone, 46 new varieties have been licensed for every major crop and area of this country.
Columbus, a new hard red spring wheat variety developed at Winnipeg, will make a major contribution. It is the first wheat variety to possess resistance to sprouting and weathering. These characteristics will make it suitable for export even in bad years when other wheats would be downgraded to a level of food grain, meaning a significant difference in income for the producers.
Gordon, a new soft white winter wheat for Ontario, was licensed in 1980. It represents a yield improvement of close to 7 per cent over Frederick and combines better winter survival and pastry quality. Columbus and Gordon then, are two major achievements in wheat breeding.
There has been progress in the breeding and improvement of other crops also. Eight new com hybrids were released. Grain corn has become a major crop in Ontario because of research which has produced better adapted hybrids and better cultural practices. Through research, corn, basically a warm-climate crop, has been grown in more and more northern latitudes and is now an important crop for Quebec, Manitoba, some parts of Alberta and the maritime provinces.
The soybean crop is one that could not have been grown in Canada to extent without research. Again, the production of a warm climate crop has been expanded because of better varieties and better cultural practices developed by the research branch of Agriculture Canada over the years. This year, Nattawa, a new variety of soybean in the intermediate maturity group, which matures up to five days earlier and yields about 10 per cent more than a standard variety, has been licensed.
Perhaps the greatest success in Canadian agricultural research is that of rapeseed. Rapeseed is an oilseed crop presently grown on more than two million hectares in Canada. It used to be grown on very limited acreage to produce a lubricating oil. Because of research it is now used to produce an edible oil and a protein supplement feed for livestock. It accounts for 40 per cent of the vegetable oil consumer in Canada.
Originally all the rapeseed varieties contained high levels of toxic materials that prevented their use in human and animal

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
nutrition. Through research, the level of these toxic materials was dramatically lowered and rapeseed became suitable for use in food and feed. A new crop and a new industry have been introduced in Canada. Edible rapeseed oil is now known as canola oil. Canola oil is used domestically and is also exported, thus improving our balance of payments.
The research bureau has been the leader in rapeseed research and has collaborated closely with universities and the industry to make rapeseed a success story. Tobin, a new canola variety, is the latest variety developed by the research bureau of Agriculture Canada. It will be licensed shortly.
In 1980 the potato breeding program at the Fredericton research station was strengthened by the addition of five professional person-years because Agriculture Canada wants Canadian potato producers to take advantage of market opportunities. I am sure the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) will be interested in that. Two new potato varieties were released in 1980.
With respect to animal production, research in progress on animal production will provide the basis for additional farm and processor incomes. Animal disease and insect control and improved feed efficiency are examples of practical problems which research has contributed to alleviating.
The foreign cattle breed evaluation program has produced interesting results in the search for faster growing, better adapted and more feed efficient beef cattle. An eight-year study demonstrated that the Hereford can be crossed with the Highland cow exceeded either parent breed in calf performance and cow productivity and proved to be an excellent range cow. Knowing there are 20 million hectares of range land in Canada, this new crossbred cow can make a significant contribution to beef production in Canada.
Land and water resource are the two natural resources on which agriculture depends. Because the food production capability of Canada's vast land mass varies so greatly, multidisciplinary teams of experts collaborate to provide information on how to make the best use of our land and how to improve its productivity. Thanks to the efforts of research branch scientists, we now grow crops on land that was part of the dust bowl of the "dirty thirties".
Water is vital to crop and animal production. In western Canada, research on the irrigation of drylands has led to increased productivity and economics in water consumption as well as to reduced salinity problems. In the east, research on soil drainage problems has permitted earlier planting and expansion of production into areas normally too wet for many crops. Plant and animal wastes are potential water polluters, but continuing research has provided practical solutions to the problem and led to the development of effective systems of waste disposal and utilization.
Energy conservation is a major concern of the research branch. Engineering research in this area covers a wide range from farm building insulation and temperature control, frequency and depth of tillage, irrigation practices and the production of fuel from animal or crop wastes. Other energy-oriented programs and biological research on the trapping of solar energy by plant and on the processes by which some plants convert nitrogen from the air into ammonia to nourish the plant. This research could result in earlier maturing plants and in savings in chemical fertilizer use.
With regard to food processing, its distribution and retailing, we find that challenging areas for research are ingredient technology, enzymology and fermentation, single cell protein, improved efficiency and waste utilization. In the area of food processing, research is directed at improving efficiency and at conserving energy. A new blancher which was scaled up from a pilot prototype developed at Kemptville, an Agriculture Canada research station, has been tested by industry. The potential energy saving is in the order of $100 per ton of processed product, a significant contribution of research to industry. Still in the food processing section, a vacuum essence concentration system designed at Summerland by Agriculture Canada has been sold on the international market. Technology transfer of a rapid continuous process for manufacturing candied fruit has resulted in the installation of a new processing line with annual capacity of 3.4 million kilograms of finished product in British Columbia. Research in the food processing sector is done in co-operation with and for industry, and it pays off.
In the area of international programs, Agriculture Canada continues to increase its contributions to international agricultural research. Being the major Canadian source of agrifood scientific, professional and technical expertise, Agriculture Canada plays an essential supportive role to the Canadian International Development Agency's activities. Canada's involvement is linked to the expectation that, in the long run, it will lead to mutually beneficial commercial relationships. Third world trade from such countries as Algeria, Nigeria, Mexico, Brazil, and others, which are giving top priority to the development of their agrifood sector, represent a medium and long-term opportunity for significant growth in Canadian sales of agricultural food and agricultural technology. Aid can promote this growth directly by the provision of Canadian goods and services which may lead to follow-up orders, and indirectly by making recipients more aware of Canadian agricultural capabilities. The expertise, knowledge and technology that Canadian scientists provide in developing countries has been developed in Canada for the use and benefit of Canadian producers and in support of Canadian industry. This excellence is recognized and used by other nations of the world.
Examples of aid programs staffed by the research bureau include wheat production in Tanzania; cereal breeding in Zambia; wheat breeding in Brazil; and fruit processing in Columbia. The India dryland project, for example, has been considered as an outstanding effort of which all Canadians should be proud.
I bring these examples of international aid programs to the attention of hon. members of this House to prove the excellence of the work of the research branch of Agriculture Canada. The expertise, knowledge and technology that
June 1, 1981

Canadian scientists provide in developing countries has been developed in Canada for the use and benefit of Canadian producers and in support of Canadian industry. This excellence is recognized and used by other nations of the world.
In closing may I say that research has contributed to the development of a strong agrifood industry in Canada. The research bureau is organized to solve current and anticipated agricultural production problems in all regions of Canada. Having qualified professional and technical staff available at short notice proves an immeasurable value in times of emergency, be it caused by a new pest or a drought.
Last year's drought for example did not cause a major disaster, even though it did cause severe problems in some areas. New tillage methods, soil conservation practices, hardier plant varieties, more experience as to which crops to plant under varying soil and climatic conditions contributed to successful farming that would have been impossible in the past. The research branch personnel compiled, and published within a few weeks, information on livestock feeding under drought conditions. Soil moisture conditions on the prairies are monitored throughout the year and advice is given on moisture reserves under stubble and fallow by crop districts as additional information in support of farmers' decisions on farming operations.
Agriculture Canada must continue to play a lead role in research and must ensure that research helps farmers in the long run through difficult times in the future.
