speechtext:
One learns a few things just by being in this House and observing the events of the day. For example, I learned on Friday from the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) that members do not offer personal greetings to family and friends from the floor of the House. I am particularly sorry because my son Gordon is in the gallery and my father Billy will this month celebrate his ninety-second birthday, a rather noteworthy occasion. It is good clean farm living that has kept him so long.
I also learned in my brief time here that 20 minutes is never as long as one anticipates. It therefore happens that much of importance that members would say is left in speech notes because time runs out. It is my intention to first list some of the positive things which this government could do for agriculture so that this government and this minister, who is so attentive to opinions of members of this House, particularly opposition members, will benefit and the nation will benefit from the advice and the direction which I offer.
Agriculture
Some government actions which are essential to both the short-term and long-term health of the agricultural sector of the Canadian economy, particularly the farmers in the area of Canada I represent, are as follows. Additional substantial financing of the Farm Credit Corporation could be part of a program of relief from the effects of extremely high interest rates. We can provide more adequate funding for agricultural research. We need relief from the proposed excise tax as it applies to the wine industry which directly affects the returns to grape growers.
We need the co-operation of all departments of government in helping to resolve the farm labour problem, particularly as it applies to itinerant and foreign labour opportunities. We need an extension of the small business development bond to unincorporated farmers, as is mentioned in the resolution. In the Okanagan we need additional funding to service the growing number of applications for cold storage construction assistance.
These are but a few of the steps, positive in nature, which this government could undertake specifically on behalf of farmers. Farmers are Canadians first and foremost and as such have a vested interest in every aspect of national policy. They would urge this government to a quick resolution of the dispute with Alberta and a radical change in attitude and policy by this government in its National Energy Program which, as constituted, is so damaging to the Canadian economy and the Canadian spirit of unity.
With world population expected to move to 10.5 billion persons by the mid point in the twenty-first century, agriculturalists world wide will be forced to make significantly greater progress in increasing food production than has ever before been previously demonstrated. In the next 70 years, to the year 2050, Third World nations must produce much more of their own food to satisfy the hunger of this expanding population whose numbers will come mainly from those countries least able to feed present populations.
In this circumstance, farmers in North America will be called upon to triple their present production over the next 40 years. The market will be there. The mouths of millions or billions of new inhabitants of this world will be opened. The challenge will be to put current know-how and future technological advances in food production into effect.
In the generations to come politicians, economists and farmers will be required to employ all of their ingenuity and skills in preventing global famine, in preventing the increased incidence of children with stomachs extended from malnutrition and to minimize the necessity for Mother Theresa, World Vision and other such selfless persons and groups to provide havens for the emaciated, starving poor of Calcultta's ghetto and other equally condemning sores in this world.
The challenge of this next century is that of a compelling necessity to return to basics in a world that has in the last century become preoccupied with more exotic pursuits. Food, clothing, shelter and water will become the imperatives superseding space exploration, armament development and transportation modes development. The imperative will be

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
simply to eat. Competition for food will replace the present world struggle based on the distribution of earth's energy supply. It will represent an exciting opportunity for Canadian agriculture.
We in Canada are fortunate to live on a continent which has prospered and developed through encouraging initiatives and ingenuities of her people. It has been the effort and skill of the individual talented and experienced farm population of Canada, not the state, which has made North America the productive empire that it is.
With less than 3 per cent of the total population of North America active in farming, each farmer today produces enough food to feed 75 persons. By the year 2000, through enhanced technology alone, individual farmers will be producing food for 200 persons. This in itself will not be sufficient. The capacity to increase total production which is available now must further increase dramatically.
In addition, expanded and improved food storage, processing and transportation methods must be developed to avoid the type of wastage presently experienced. Water storage, distribution and conservation must be improved. Research into more efficient use of water in agriculture is an absolute necessity, even in water rich Canada.
This is a primary essential in the Okanagan valley, a fruit producing area with an average rainfall of only ten inches annually. Even in metric measure that is dry. However, we can meet the challenge in Canada. It is simply a matter of improving farm economics and the provision of a rational political climate in which to operate, both of which are jeopardized by the attitude of this government.
The family farm is basic to B.C.'s fruit and grape production. The family farm has proved to be a more efficient producer than either the corporate or the collective farm under any political jurisdiction. One need only compare the entrepreneurial family farm concern concept with its continued increasing productivity to that of the U.S.S.R. Under the collective farm system, communist nations have gone from net exporters to net importers of foodstuffs. Poland's current problems are largely a result of that hard fact. Collectivity stifles productive enterprises and inhibits progress. The role of the state is to encourage, not control productive unions. A stable farm income is the prime goal. The most prominent income problems facing Canadian farmers today are financing the acquisition capital and financing the cost of production, or paying for farm and equipment and then paying for its operation.
The minister is quoted as having stated recently in a speech that debt charges are the second largest farm cost, and the cost of money has gone up 2.5 times faster than any other commodity farmers have to work with. The question is, knowing that, what is the minister doing to help the situation which he describes?
The minister today in his speech pointed with proprietary pride to the buoyant nature of B.C. agriculture. I think that is
a dangerous generalization. Without attempting to minimize the federal contribution made to the B.C. farming community in the form of ARDA, cash advances, cold storage construction grants, crop insurance, stabilization, etc., I must note that the chief distinction which marks B.C. agriculture is the B.C. government farm income insurance program. It is this provincial program which has created the optimism and vigour presently being experienced in B.C., and for this neither this minister nor this government can claim credit.
The compounding effect of high inflation and high interest rates is the foremost deterrent to farm efficiency and management at a time when farm production needs to be encouraged and strengthened. A 10 per cent annual inflation rate results in cost increases of more than 2.5 times in ten years. A 15 per cent inflation rate equates to a fourfold increase in cost inputs in that same period. This is the circumstance imposed by this government, and with this reverse incentive how will the farmer possibly be able to meet the demand for greater production?
Officials of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada recently called on government to moderate interest rates, reach an oil pricing agreement with Alberta, to reduce government spending, and restore consumer confidence. Similar advice has come from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, representatives of small business associations and farmer groups.
David Slater, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, told the Commons finance committee that Governor Bouey is having to go it alone in the fight against inflation because the government has no other anti-inflation policy in place. Mr. Slater said that a combination of policies might allow inflation to be dealt with and at the same time the real performance of the economy to be improved; advice offered to unhearing ears.
This government shows no sense of real restraint in its spending. Waste and neglect are its marks, patronage and self-aggrandization its tools. It is irresponsible government within Canada that is the root cause of inflation and high interest rates. We are captive of U.S. interest rates only because the government opposite chooses short-term political expediency over national well-being. That is why farm bankruptcies have increased by 77 per cent. That is why the younger generation of orchardists in the Okanagan are finding they cannot pursue their chosen vocation, some losing substantial investments. We are witnessing the destruction of hopes, the burying of ambition, the demoralizing effect of financial disasters created by careless and irresponsible action beyond the farmer's control.
Farm and Country headlines today read "Foreclosure rate soars", "Cruel interest rates take bigger toll than ever". Inside it states:
That is the problem we have now: an horrendous 12 per cent inflation rate, and an even more horrendous interest rate of 19 per cent. You see, gentle reader, no one has confidence in our ability to handle money.
June 1, 1981

Later it states:
The only possible answer is tough federal action to bring about a balanced budget. Not this year, not next-because the sudden dislocation would cause too much hardship-but over the next three to five years.
That is what the Farm and Country says.
In the riding I represent, the Keremeos Co-op Growers Association and Similkameen United Growers Association are closing down their fruit packing facilities. At the present cost of borrowing, the move to keep abreast of modern technological advances in fruit handling is beyond the growers' financial capacity. As a result, the town of Keremeos with a population of only some 2,000 people is about to lose its major payroll, an annual loss to the business community of more than $1.5 million. This is the impact on only one community, a community which can ill afford such a knock.
We on this side of the House have been saying repeatedly that the need is to set proper and productive priorities in spending, not increase spending as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) so frequently states. Why in the name of nationalism spend $1.5 billion, sending it out of the country to purchase a string of service stations which add not one barrel of additional production to Canada's oil capacity? It would be much better for Canada to have put that $1.5 billion, raised from long-suffering Canadians, into aspects of research and development, into cold storage assistance, into helping the Naramata irrigation district and others in equal distress to finance the upgrading of their water works. By all means, why not use the $1.5 billion to improve the role of the Farm Credit Corporation in helping Canadian farmers to meet the challenges in food production which Canada and this world face now and in the future?
The May 30 issue of The Financial Post front paged the story of a $2 million ultramodern hog farm within 20 miles of Ottawa which will be bankrupt by this weekend. The article elaborates:
The federal government has been taking it on the chin over the outcry at the rising tide of farm bankruptcies-
It goes on to state:
But there are indications from federal officials that Whelan put up a tough fight in cabinet for some sort of interest rate relief. He lost-
That is clout for you. It goes on to state:
But there's ample pressure on MacEachen to give ground.
Later it states:
The normally diplomatic and staid Canadian Federation of Agriculture has come out with a tough statement asking the government to use the federal Farm Credit Corp. to solve the problem.
It then states:
The FCC argues that the money should not detract from MacEachen's economic gradualism because it ought to be seen as an investment. The farmers would be paying it back. Treating it as expenditure in the federal budget is incorrect, says CFA Executive Director David Kirk.
It goes on to state:
-Ontario farmers are asking the Crown corporation to take over short-term and medium-term debt held by the banks and count it as long-term.
Agriculture
-FCC dislikes doing this, but has always had a policy allowing it in extreme cases. And there's no question that some farmers need that help now-
There is a positive suggestion for the minister. Spare some farmer the trauma of bankruptcy by long-term refinancing of present short-term debt through the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has asked that additional funding be put into the Farm Credit Corporation to broaden the funding base immediately, and in light of the fact that farm bankruptcies have increased dramatically, time is of the essence. Additional funding is imperative.
On another matter, I would ask through you, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture get together with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to come to grips with the problem of temporary worker permits for farm workers visiting from other countries. The British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association and the Canadian Horticultural Council requested such, and while the minister expressed sympathy while attending the BCFGA convention in Kelowna last January, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has said no.
I have many more things that I would like to say but I will leave the matter of the excise tax until the debate on that subject later in the week.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating a motion censuring the government for failing to stop the increase in interest rates which have now become unacceptable to farmers. I agree that high interest rates may temporarily put farmers in a financial strait-jacket, but I suggest that we should have a look at what the minister and the Department of Agriculture are doing for Canadian farmers to protect them, and perhaps also at the level of productivity recorded in recent years by the farming community in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am a front line advocate of the interests of our agricultural producers. This is why at the sittings of the agriculture committee 1 had asked how our taxation system applied to agricultural producers as compared with Canadian industrialists. At that time I had even suggested that the more dynamic producers in Canada be given an option to benefit from a farm loans accelerated repayment plan. Here is an example: I had then proposed that a farmer with a $200,000 loan repayable at the annual rate of $10,000 over a 20-year period, plus interests, be allowed to pay back $1,000, $2,000 or up to $5,000 a year without considering that additional repayment as an income so as to prompt the farmer into speeding up his payments to the Farm Credit Corporation, in turn making it possible for the FCC to have the funds required to make accelerated repayment loans to other agricultural producers. There is a shortage right now. The Farm Credit Corporation is already strapped for funds and we have hardly gone through six months of operations this year.

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
Mr. Speaker, that is perhaps a very significant factor. We might examine even further what would be the consequences of such a proposal. True, the interest rate went up 2 per cent lately. I am convinced that this additional 2 per cent will not push Canadian farmers into bankruptcy since the market value of a farm has already jumped by 18 per cent this year. Hon. members will agree with me that the agricultural producer's goodwill is growing ever higher.
I think we should all consider together the tools the Canadian government could provide the farmer with in order to improve his efficiency in these difficult but hopefully temporary times we are now going through in this country. I, for one, Mr. Speaker, wish the farmer was urged to modernize his operation and even use computers which would allow him, through a terminal, to keep constantly in touch with his accountant. Let me explain. The data would be transmitted to an accounting and management centre where complex accounting, feasibility and other data would be collected. On a technical level, crop rotation, work schedules, and irrigation, fertilization, selection and even feeding tables could be established. Even environmental or weather fluctuations could be programmed. A great deal of information which is very timeconsuming to record could be regularly updated. Also, since our greatest weakness in agriculture has always been marketing, the information expert could keep the farmer daily informed of market fluctuations. The computer could even be used to monitor various things, for instance, to program animal feed or fertilization. This could allow a stricter control of the major and the minor components. Such expert programming could even result in a decrease in acreage, resulting in energy savings.
Mr. Speaker, 1 have this past year spent many hours sitting on the Committee on Agriculture. Recently, when we were considering the goverment's agricultural and food policies, 1 realized that several members, mostly from the opposition, did not understand how modern agriculture should develop in this country. While we were reviewing financial papers, we realized that many members asked serious questions, for instance, if the money spent on the agri-food industry actually benefited the farmers. The modern farmer must have up-to-date tools at his disposal. And I believe that the best tools are marketing and the development of new varieties, since marketing is a weakness in several sectors of agriculture in Canada. 1 have noticed this weakness in several productions, for instance western beef, which is world famous and which is certainly not marketed properly in eastern Canada. I believe that no money was ever spent to market or promote this excellent Canadian product and praise its nutritional value, which could increase sales on the Canadian market.
Take, for example, the dairy policy in Ontario and Quebec. 1 remember that a few years ago we had a surplus of millions of pounds of powdered milk and millions of pounds of butter, which meant millions in storage costs. Because of a firm policy and the establishment of quotas in 1975, which nearly caused a small revolution among Canadian producers, some restraint was put on dairy production. The producers decided jointly
with the provincial and Canadian governments to launch a national publicity campaign to promote the merits and the sales of dairy products. Believe it or not, sales of dairy products in Canada have increased by 4 per cent this year. This is what I call a modern tool. Experts are hired to promote Canadian products in the country.
Another example is Canadian pork, which has the reputation of being the best in the world on international markets. The proof of this is that we export for about $200 million of pork to the United States every year. I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to underline these positive achievements of our Canadian producers. A while ago, I was listening to the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), who blamed the government for its bad policies and for causing concern among farmers. I have doubts about this. If we had implemented the opposition's energy policy and paid world prices for our oil, 1 am convinced that it would have been much more harmful than the 2 per cent interest we are now paying, because farm loans amount to approximately $300,000 on the average in Canada, and if I am not mistaken, at a rate of 2 per cent, this means $6,000 in interest, and energy costs on a specialized farm would be much more than $6,000 at current world prices.
Mr. Speaker, I would not want some people to spread fear among our farm producers. For the informaiton of my colleague opposite, I also note that when I was in the opposition, the government removed the subsidies for building vegetable storage facilities. Canadian producers should thank the Minister of Agriculture for having reinstated these subsidies in order to help them take a greater share of the market instead of importing farm products as we did for so many years in Canada.
I should also like to mention all that is being done in agriculture with regard to quality, inspection, processing, storage, and as I have already said, research on pesticides. I had the opportunity of looking closely at the general research division whose general terms of reference were as follows:
To work toward the establishment of efficient, stable and profitable agriculture in Canada.
I am sure all hon. members in this House agree on the basic principles of the general research division.
To ensure that the essential natural resources of agriculture are wisely explored conserved, used and managed.
I also feel, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members should make it their duty to study carefully what the general research division is doing for our Canadian agriculture. I am sure that many doubts would thus be dispelled from their minds.
Now Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to deal with stabilization programs. We saw the government act to stabilize potato prices during two consecutive years, because producers were selling their potatoes below the average cost. We recently saw the Canadian government stabilize pork prices to the tune of some $112 million. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the government cannot do everything alone, and perhaps the Canadian pork industry may not have such influ-
June 1, 1981

ence on the global price of pork as some may believe. But although the Agricultural Stabilization Act does not meet the expectations of Canadian producers 100 per cent, I feel the program is very generous, and having talked with a number of pork producers in Quebec, I must indicate they all agreed that such an offer from the Canadian government was very acceptable and very welcome.
There is something of interest to me which we might discuss together, namely the valuation of quotas. Clearly it will be recognized that the matter of quotas is very important to farmers, and there is an increasing need for farm product quotas to stabilize production. There is, however, a question I would put to every member in this House. It is whether we are going to give some value to that quota, because young people wanting to become farmers are already complaining about the excessive price of farms. It will be recognized that if quotas are valued at some $100,000, $150,000 or $200,000, it is almost impossible for any farmer to return to farming, or for young people to get into farming. I therefore feel that this matter should be very closely examined by everyone who shares an interest in Canadian farming. And in any discussion of the dairy policy, a good look should be taken at what Canfarm has accomplished, because Canfarm has been a very modern tool which made it possible for producers to monitor their milk production very closely through a computer program. We know that tremendous progress was accomplished in that area, and all Canadian producers in that industry should be commended for having been world pioneers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to conclude without referring to prospects of food prices. In that regard, we should give credit to our Canadian farmers for their efficiency. Most Canadians are unaware that on average, in spite of inflation, today they are not spending a larger percentage of their income to buy food than ten years ago. Indeed, their personal income has increased more quickly than food prices during the last decade. In addition, Canadians spend a lesser percentage of their disposable income for food than people in any other country in the world, except the United States which, it must be stated, is the only country in the world where food is produced throughout the year. As indicated in the following table, in 1979 Canadians have devoted an average of 13 per cent of their disposable income, necessarily after taxes, to purchase food to be consumed at home and 4.3 per cent to meals taken outside for a total of 17.3 per cent against 17.7 per cent in 1971. However, it must be recognized that our low-wage earners or individuals on fixed pensions pay a higher percentage. American consumers alone spend a lesser part of their disposable income on food, that is about 16.1 per cent. In 1979, according to the Department of Agriculture of the United States, taking into account our more limited market and our shorter farming season, Canadian farmers, producers and food distributors had an outstanding performance. According to two international studies, food prices in Canada are lower than in most other countries. A study carried out in April, 1980, by the United States Department of Agriculture indicated that, expressed in Canadian dollars, a food basket
Agriculture
with 18 items cost $50.85 in Ottawa, $45.32 in Washington, $66.89 in London and $82.17 in Paris. A study by the Bank of Switzerland confirmed the Canadian consumers' favourable position and indicated that a basket with over 39 items cost $134 in Montreal, $149 in Toronto, $191 in Brussels, and $223 in Geneva. Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied Canadian producers will maintain their effectiveness, provided they keep on getting from our Department of Agriculture the tools they need so badly. Although I may recognize that the current high interest rates may hurt our farmers temporarily-a 2 per cent increase, for instance-I am sure Canadian producers will fight back and demonstrate their effectiveness as usual.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for putting forward this motion which we are debating today. I believe agriculture is one of the topics we do not discuss enough in this House. We do not give a high enough priority to it. I also believe that agriculture is the No. 1 industry in this country and the most important industry in the world. It is one that is undergoing very rapid change in technological devices, as the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) has just finished saying. It is one which will be very important in the years ahead as the world population continues to explode. What we need at this time, Mr. Speaker, is some long-term thinking about where we are going as a nation, where we are going as a world and what we will do for our farmers to ensure we feed the world's people. I believe that some of today's problems were caused by the shortsightedness of the people who guided our policies in yesteryear.
When I hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) get up and speak, as he did today, I am a little bit disappointed because he uses the line that everything in this country is the greatest, that we have the greatest policies in agriculture, that we have the greatest this and the greatest that, and the greatest minister of agriculture. To listen to the minister you would think the panacea is here, that he has reached Utopia and that the milennium is here. I find that thinking a little bit dangerous, because when someone thinks that everything is being done, then that person ceases to be useful in the function he is supposed to perform. It reminds me a little of Mohammed Ali, the old fighter who used to say, "I am the greatest." That worked for about 15 years when, suddenly, he stepped into the ring and met Larry Holmes, and he was out on the eleventh round. Maybe it is about time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) reassessed the Minister of Agriculture and placed in that position someone who would think innovatively, someone who could think of some alternatives with regard to where we are going.
It is all right to boast a little. We have a lot to be proud of in this country. I disagree with the minister when he never ceases to boast, and when he never seems to come up with any new ideas We have a great many productive farmers in Canada, farmers who have done a great deal for our nation over the

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
years, farmers who have increased their productivity faster than any other sector in the country, whether it be the workers of Canada, the manufacturing sector, or what have you. They have provided a base. 1 believe that we are now at an important crossroads. We must ask ourselves where we are going. We must ask ourselves where the farm community is headed. I believe the farmer needs some protection in terms of the price he receives for the commodity he sells. We need to improve our stabilization plans so that a farmer knows in the spring what he will receive for his product when he reaps it at harvest time. We need more marketing boards. Earlier today the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) said that the farmer is the only person left in our society who is supposed to live by the so-called free enterprise system-and it is not working. It is not free. It is the small farmer who suffers. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer needs similar protection to the worker through unions or through professional associations such as doctors and lawyers have, or through such organizations as the Manufacturers' Association. They need similar protection to the groups I have mentioned by banding together to form marketing boards which are producer-controlled. In this way they will receive for their product a fair value for the work they put into it and for the capital they invest in it.
In this country we have four good examples of national marketing boards. They are the chicken, the turkey, the milk and egg marketing boards. Even though these marketing boards are not perfect, and I have many criticisms of them, such as the price of quota-

My friend the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) has already indicated that the price of quotas in Canada is already too high for ordinary people, and I fully agreed with him when he said that we need a review of our quota policy in Canada.

Despite that we can learn a great deal from these national marketing boards. We can extend them to have them producer-controlled for all products in Canada. 1 believe that should come about when the producers want it, through their own democratic elections in their own organizations.
In terms of prices, the government must back up the Crow rate. It must preserve the Crow rate in this country which the farmers fought for over so many years. This rate has benefited the Canadian wheat farmer for decades.
I turn now to the question of expenses. Earlier today the hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned many of the problems farmers have when it comes to high interest rates, the cost of farm machinery and the cost of land. I have before me a couple of letters I received from two farmers, and I think they tell the story. One is from a dairy farmer in Ontario who says that in 1980 the interest on his loan was $26,000. In 1981, on that same loan, the farmer will pay some $58,000 in interest. The second letter is from a farmer in central Saskatchewan. Last year he had a loan on which he paid interest at 10 per cent, or $16,000. This year on the same loan the
interest rate has doubled, it is 20 per cent. He will be paying some $32,000 in interest to the financial institutions of this country. This same farmer says that to meet his interest alone on 80 acres of land-half of a quarter section which he has in seed this year-the price of wheat would have to fetch $8 a bushel to finance the interest on a $60,000 loan. The price of a bushel of wheat now is about $7. Aside from the interest, he has fuel costs, living expenses, repairs, clothing and food for his family and everything else a farmer needs to live.
When I see statistics of this kind, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the government is not more humane, why it does not place some controls on the banks to ensure that in this country we have a two-interest rates policy, a lower rate for the necessities of life, such as housing and farming, and a higher rate for unproductive borrowing for non-essentials such as television sets and the like. I have no idea why the Minister of Agriculture, who pretends to speak for the farmers, is not able to persuade the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister to introduce such a policy, to force the banks to roll back interest rates for the necessities of life in our country. Instead, under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture, farmers see less and less money being lent to them by the Farm Credit Corporation. In 1980-81, some $516 million was available to farmers. In this year, 1981-82, the sum is down to $500 million. In 1979-80, $628 million was available to farmers. So instead of making more money available to farmers at lower interest rates and putting it at the disposal of people who are productive, who produce goods which will go into the collective value of goods and services for all the people of Canada, we see the government doing the reverse of what I call sane and putting aside less money, despite the fact that farmers are in a severe financial pinch.
The other costs about which I think we must do something very shortly are the costs of land, the price of land and the size of farms. How large are we going to allow farms to become before we finally say, "Stop it. It is big enough"? It is big enough because large farms are not necessarily more productive. It is big enough because large farms mean fewer farmers and the destruction of a rural and family farm way of life. Bigger farms mean that there will be fewer and fewer villages and towns in the rural parts of this country. The time is going to come when we will have to make some pretty tough decisions in this country about the size of farms. It is about time that this House and the farmers of Canada started to put some thought toward an answer to that very difficult question.
The other matter is the price of land. A farmer the other day bought a quarter of a section of land near Regina for $60,000. A bit farther away, another farmer purchased a half section of land for $130,000. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, when is it going to stop? When is the wild and mad speculation in land going to stop, or are we going to have a crash in land prices in the next year or two like the one we had in 1929, like the crash in the stock exchange?
June 1, 1981

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext: How would you stop a Canadian from buying national land?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House leader of the Conservative party asked a very good question. How will one stop a Canadian from buying land and driving up the price of land? I do not pretend to know the answers to that kind of question, but I think that it is a question which we will have to address as a Parliament because the price of land, today, in my part of the world, is going out of the reach of the ordinary person, the ordinary guy. I understand it is happening in central Canada as well. We will have to come up with a solution to the high price of land. 1 would like to see the Minister of Agriculture decide to introduce some policies and some discussions about the high price of land and do something about it.
Perhaps, as the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquit-lam (Miss Jewett) has just mentioned, we should introduce more programs in other provinces and nationally, as we have in Saskatchewan where we have a land bank program. Maybe that is part of the answer. Perhaps we should have a prices review board which looks at whether prices are being inflated artificially.
Perhaps we should change our laws regarding speculation, because one of the problems we are having today is that some foreigners are coming in and they do not really care what the price of land is. They have the money to pay for it and the interest rates do not really matter that much. They can write it off. Many Canadians who are not genuine farmers have that attitude. I am referring to people who are wealthy, have a few bucks and can buy a half section of land for $130,000 or $150,000. They could write it off as a tax expense, and this drives up the price of land to the ordinary farmer who needs it and cannot afford it.
Anyway, I think these are some of the questions we are going to have to address. If we do not do it soon, we will end up in this country with larger and larger farms, fewer and fewer rural communities and perhaps corporate farms such as they have in the state of Colorado where the whole rural way of life is destroyed. They are moving into another era where corporations are doing the farming, where farm workers are working the land, and another set of problems comes along with that. I think these are some of the problems that are facing the farmer.
In my remaining five or six minutes, I want to stress that it is important that we solve some of these problems because I think agriculture is very important to all of Canada. It is very important to the consumers of this nation. We have to be more self-sufficient in agriculture if we are going to stop some of the ups and downs in the pricing that we have today. Most Canadians do not realize what would happen if we took away grain and oil seeds in this country. In 1980, we were a net importer of food to the tune of around $2 billion. Many of those foods we are importing, such as beef and many others.
We could easily be self-sufficient if we had government policies which would help the farmers plan their production. Policies could be co-ordinated with provincial governments
Agriculture
toward a goal of self-sufficiency in food production in Canada at as local a level as possible so that when ordinary people buy food as consumers they could purchase fresh food near a farm, food which had not been transported great distances and would not have diminished nutritive value which results from being taken off the farm or out of a garden for a long period of time.
I also think, from the consumer's point of view, that much more effort must be put into a nutritious food policy for Canada. We have had many changes in our food system over the last 30 years since the Second World War. We have more and more additives and chemicals in foods; hundreds of them today. We have artificial and manufactured foods. There is more and more evidence that what we are doing to our food system is affecting our health. It may be the cause of some of our modern cancers and different types of heart disease that we have in this country and around the world which we cannot cure. I believe the government must once again take the initiative and do some imaginative thinking about a nutritious food policy for Canada. To repeat what some farmers have suggested, perhaps there could be a labelling program for organic produce and subsidizing or aiding farmers who want to grow foods organically. We should do more research. As my friend, the hon. member for Chicoutimi said, we should do research into the effect of chemicals on our food systems and see whether we can produce more efficiently foods which are more healthy without the use of a lot of chemicals which are very hazardous, not only to human life, but to plant life and also to the life of the soil which deteriorates over a period of time.
These are some of the problems that we have as Canadians. We are going to have to solve them very, very shortly before the possibility of a solution evades us. I do not say that lightly. There has been a recent report by a doctor in Saskatchewan, a soil scientist-I believe his name is Dr. Reny-who said that in our own province, through the lack of proper summer-fallow, the lack of irrigation in places, the lack of proper safeguards of rotating crops, tree lines and so on, and the use of chemicals and the like, the quality of our soil has deteriorated by about 50 per cent in, I believe, the last 30, 40 or 50 years.
If we do not start looking at some of these problems and if we do not start producing for tomorrow and tomorrow's generation instead of always producing for today and looking at today's dollar, then the time will come when we will not be capable of being self-sufficient in many parts of our country. If we do not start solving the problems of acid rain and understanding what it has already done to some of the crop line in southwestern Ontario and what it may do with the aid of the tar sands plants in the prairies and the wheat fields of the prairies, then, indeed, there will be a sad chapter for the future of the human race.
Those problems affect Canada and they will also affect the world. In terms of the world, I have always believed that we are a global family, that we are our brother's keeper, that we must do for others what we want for ourselves, and we must
10148

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
provide for people in Africa, Asia, China and all around the world the kinds of policies that we want for ourselves in this country.
In my opinion we have an obligation to do two things. We have an obligation to help other countries to become self-sufficient in the production of food. I believe we can do that because in this country we develop a lot of agricultural and food technology which is among the most advanced in the world. I think we have an obligation to use it to help other countries feed themselves and to put bread on the tables of hungry families. 1 do not think there is a country in the world, with perhaps three or four exceptions, that with proper irrigation and planning, and a bit of assistance from such countries as ours, cannot feed themselves.
We must also participate more in food aid programs where food aid is needed. However, we must never forget that we should not constantly just hand out food aid without trying to help people to help themselves. It is very important that we teach people to be self-sufficient.
As my friend, the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) says, we must all get away from importing luxury goods from Third World countries which we do not need and which they produce on the best land that they have. They are taking the most productive land in Guatemala, or other places in the world, and sowing crops like bananas and tobacco on it and exporting to us. Meanwhile, their own people go hungry because they are producing their food or whatever they can on secondary land. Situations like that must change, and our country and our government can take a leadership role toward that end.
A friend of mine has said that to feed the world, to provide adequate water to the world, to educate the world's people and to provide them with health services, we would need an additional $17 billion per year. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker-about as much as the world spends on arms every two weeks. It is spent on nuclear warheads, fighter planes, bombs, tanks, shells, guns and ammunition. It is enough to destroy the world many times over, whether it is done by the Russians, the Americans or any other country in the world. The madness goes on, the attempt of one to better the other. The madness might come to an end if countries like Canada would take the initiative as a respected middle power and say to the world that we must spend this money, the know-how and the technology we have to feed the world's people, to house and educate them and to provide adequate medical care for them.
I say to the minister, in conclusion, that we can start tonight. We are a great country. We have done great things and we are only beginning. If we realize that, we can do exciting things for our farmers, for our people and for the people of the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in speaking this evening in this debate. My experience in agriculture has not been limited to that of practising my profession. In any case, I am proud to be one who has been of some service to the agriculture industry in this country.
The farmer needs help but he needs different kinds of help. For example, he is probably the most misunderstood person in our community. He produces a perishable product and he produces a biological product. Many businessmen are upset if they are stuck with inventory and have no way of getting rid of it, but at least they can pack it away until the next season. If fall clothes are not sold this year, they can be put away until next fall. The farmer cannot do that with his produce. He is stuck with it. Sometimes he does not have enough and sometimes has too much, and so it is very difficult to cope. He has to be a small businessman, a big businessman and an agri-businessman.
Some suggestions have been made today relative to our minister. I should like to say that his has probably the most difficult ministry in government. He has a great urban group to contend with that does not really understand very much about the difficulties of agriculture. He has to talk for the farmer and he has to act for the farmer. I should like to go on record as saying that in my experience I think our minister does a good talking job and a good acting job. He certainly does his very best to convince members of the government and the people of Canada that the farmer is somebody who really is somebody.
Some reference has been made today to the fact that we should have a fourth veterinary college in Canada, situated in the maritimes. A report was commissioned from the former dean of the Ontario Veterinary College, Dennis Howell. I should like to read from his report as follows:
Setting aside the contribution which a fourth school would make to the manpower needs of Canada, it must be remembered that, currently, an area of Canada where animal industry, both aquatic and terrestrial, dominates the economy is devoid of an animal health educational resource. In almost every brief submitted the opinion was expressed that a veterinary school located in one of the Atlantic provinces would add a much needed dimension to the livestock industry of the region by virtue of its scholarly activity, its research program and its inevitable role in professional refreshment. A second and no less significant point is: Can the young people of the Atlantic region continue to be denied, subtantially, the opportunity to fulfil their career objectives?
It follows, of course, that you cannot give this type of service to agriculture, with both the teaching facility and research facility, without the necessary faculty. There is considerable doubt about whether we should be robbing the other veterinary colleges in Canada in order to supply the necessary manpower to a fourth school. I think the following comment in the report is relative:
In general, veterinary medicine lacks opportunities comparable to those enjoyed by the medical schools of Canada under the programs of the Medical Research Council.
The exception to this is a fellowship program under the Medical Research Council which has been particularly useful for research in veterinary medicine. The report continues:
What is needed is a program, possibly administered by Agriculture Canada through the medium of the Agricultural Research Council, designed to train

young veterinarians at various levels for future academic careers. Such a program should include summer studentships for undergraduates, scholarships for graduate studies, and fellowships for graduate studies, and fellowships for study in a post-doctoral sense. The stipends need to be attractive and should be at the same rates provided by the Medical Research Council for its comparable programs.
This government has shown a fair amount of leadership in trying to establish a fourth veterinary college. I believe that we will see it in the future and that it will provide the necessary service to make sure that our animal industry in particular is provided with the kind of diagnostic service and care which will make the economical production of livestock possible.
I am sure that my colleagues from the west can recall the days when we tried to establish a third veterinary college in Canada. It was finally established ten years ago and was called the Western Veterinary College. We had the same doubts then about whether it was feasible to establish another faculty of veterinary medicine to serve the agricultural industry in Canada. We had all the same questions about where we would get the faculty, whether there would be enough jobs for the graduates, and whether it was feasible to support it. Of course, we met the same kind of arguments and in many cases the conclusions were that we would be foolish to attempt to establish this very expensive school for training veterinarians for the future.
I am pleased to say that with the co-operation of the western provinces and the federal government, which supplied 50 per cent of the necessary funds, the third veterinary school was established in Saskatoon. Within a very short time it became one of the finest veterinary colleges in Canada. It has sent graduates all over the world and I am proud to say that it has proven to be a good investment in animal health.
Recently, I travelled with the North-South task force in various Asian countries. I was very pleased to see the number of graduates in agricultural and veterinary science that there are in the Third World as the result of their training in Canada. As far as agriculture is concerned, I like to think that our profession has served well and valiantly through the years. I hope that the fourth veterinary college will be established. Some kind of fellowship program could be set up to help provide the necessary faculty so that our agricultural industry in Canada will be the leader because of the kind of support it receives.
Probably many of you do not know that we in Canada have a reputation around the world for having healthy livestock, which means that markets are open to us because we have been able to keep out those diseases which ravage livestock in many other countries. We do this by maintaining an animal population free of disease. We have inspection services which are able to spot immediately when a disease has been brought into the country. We get rid of this disease by eliminating it. Therefore, we are free of diseases such as foot and mouth and hog cholera. Obviously one disease affects hogs and the other affects livestock. These two diseases are the scourge of many countries in the world. Canadian livestock is welcome almost
Agriculture
everywhere in the world because of our high health standards. I do not want to take all the credit for the veterinarians but this standard is maintained because of the very fine management provided by farmers not only through their training in agriculture but through the usual Canadian ability to do things and to do them properly. However, this standard could not be maintained without the kind of veterinarian support they receive.
I think we can be proud of our inspection service. We can be proud of the fact that all our animals, because of their good health, are acceptable in almost every country in the world.
1 am sure hon. members know that to be a veterinarian requires a very long training program. But looking at the total agricultural picture, it is a case of everyone working together to make sure that our animal industry is the finest that is possible. To my hon. friend who spoke before me I want to say that we have the finest agricultural industry in the world. With development of confidence, with service programs, particularly relating to animal health, which I am proud to say the present government supports and in which the minister is showing great leadership by promoting these activities in Canada, we will go on with a very fine agricultural industry. In spite of our problems with credit, in spite of the fact that we are producing perishable goods, in spite of the fact that we have a biological product, in spite of the fact that some farmers want help and some do not, in spite of the fact that we do not have unanimity as to what programs there should be to help farmers, there is no question that our government is convinced that farmers are very important people in Canada. The agricultural industry is the basis of our tremendous growth. Canada is the great country it is today because we have a healthy, vibrant and strong agricultural industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY. S.O. 58-EFFECTS ON AGRICULTURE INDUSTRY OF HIGH INTEREST RATE POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Guelph (Mr. Schroder) for sharing part of his time with me so that I could close the debate.
The first part of my remarks are what I intend to say at the end of my speech, namely that today's debate, and I have listened to all of it, has been rather depressing for one like myself. I know that one of the healthiest industries in Canada is the agricultural industry. I know that the opportunity for agriculture has never been greater than it is now. I know that the world wants to be fed and insists on being fed. I know that farmers not only produce the food for our table but also will soon be producing the energy to keep us warm at night. The future for agriculture is unbelievable. Whether we worry about big farms or small farms, the fact is we are moving toward intensive and more efficient agriculture because there is a need for it. If we could get these people in Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces to realize that they have a job to do and could make some money, we would soon get this agricultural industry going even better than it is today.
Unfortunately, at times snags are put in our way. Governments have done much for the agricultural industry in this country. I think the U.S. government has done very well for its farmers too. We have done a good job for agriculture, but the

June 1, 1981
Agriculture
job is never finished. Right at the present we have a dark cloud hanging over our heads. Some nitwits in the central banks of the world, backed up by the nitwits in the departments of finance, are determined to prove that although the book learning they acquired 40 years ago is not working out, they will show it to be correct. They think if they get the interest rates high enough, all the things they studied will come true. But quantitative evidence shows just the opposite. I will not make a speech about that tonight because I want to talk about the particular subject before us.
This subject tonight really deals with farm credit. Sure the small business development bond will be a big help. I hope the government will broaden it out to cover wider sources than just the incorporated farmers. My main topic tonight is the Farm Credit Corporation. We have had a long history of credit on the farms in Canada. I will not repeat what I said before as to what happened in 1919 in that great debacle or what happened in the 1930s and what was done by all governments in an effort to solve those crises because that is past history.
If we are going to meet the challenge today of feeding the world and keeping the world warm through the production of energy from renewable resources, we have to use supplies of credit. We are based on a credit system. If we are to have this silliness of a group of academic dropouts who man our departments of finance and who man our central banks around the world telling politicians what they have to do when they know it is wrong, that it has always been wrong and it still is wrong, then we have to depend on the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to speak up on this subject in cabinet.

speechtext:
I know that it has been said that he has enough clout. Believe me, if you ever want to have clout in the cabinet, just offer to resign and tell the people why you are resigning. All of a sudden 25 or 30 other guys in cabinet say "no, don't do that". But all you have to do is to put your resignation on the table. There is not a prime minister born now or in the future who would ever turn down a minister of agriculture, if you want to unite the people of Canada around an issue, that issue is interest rates.
The interest rate issue goes back thousands of years. In Canada it has taken our Parliament by the throat on several occasions. If you want to unite farmers from Newfoundland to Quebec right through to British Columbia, just fool around with this nonsense on interest rates. You can bring every farmer together. They could clean out 70 different members of Parliament if they wanted to. I simply ask the Minister of Agriculture to pay attention to some of the positive and helpful ideas which have emanated from this side of the House over the last two weeks.
Hon. members heard today from the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave). He put forward his concept of an individual trust system whereby the farmer in his surplus years puts his cash into a trust account. No subsidy from the government is required. He just wants to have that money available when the income is poor. It would not cost the
government anything. The hon. member went on this afternoon to suggest putting this money directly into the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation, who act as a trustee, instead of putting it into a bank or a credit union. The farmers would be glad to put money into a farm credit trust fund at 6 per cent because they will not be taxed on it. The Farm Credit Corporation could lend that money out at 8 per cent and get the young farmers up and going. Get rid of this high interest rate of 20 per cent a year and above. This is not a laughing matter that will go away next week by dropping the interest rate a point or two. Anything above 6 or 8 per cent on the productive side of our economy is lunacy. The quickest way to get it down without a subsidy by the government is to lend the money at 8 per cent. Ask the farmers to put their money into a trust account under the hands of the Farm Credit Corporation and get 6 per cent. As long as the farmer is free of tax, he will accept that 6 per cent. Not only the beef farmer but the grain farmer will do that. He will not want any subsidy when he is saving tax. He knows that money will be available when his income is low and he can take it back as income.
If that idea of loans is put before cabinet with all the enthusiasm a minister of agriculture can mount, he will have
350,000	farmers from all across the country behind him. The minute he does that, just watch the banks and credit unions get their interest rates down for every other class of people.
This is not a question of grabbing money out of the treasury. The treasury does not have any. They are borrowing like mad to pay the high price of oil. This is a positive proposal by an opposition member who has made this type of proposal before. It was originally introduced in this House some years ago by the then hon. member for Swift Current. He is not here tonight. It has been improved on and made more powerful in the way the hon. member for Medicine Hat repeated it. According to this concept, if you are going to stablize the income of any farmer, you let him have an account he can put his money into when he has a surplus. He can earn money when it is needed. He only pays the tax on it when he draws it as income.
This is an individual accounting system which does not require 10,000 civil servants to examine every item. It is a matter between him and a trustee. When the farmer puts the money into that account, he entrusts the trustee to use it for a proper purpose, to earn money and to be useful to his country. At the same time, when he wants it, it is available.
The suggestion made this afternoon that the Farm Credit Corporation handle it makes eminent good sense. The farmer could be told to put money into the trust account where he would receive 6 per cent. It could then be loaned to other farmers who need it badly at 8 per cent.
The farmer gets a better, more saleable proposal than the one I made last week. Last week I proposed that we lend money through the Farm Credit Corporation at 8 per cent. When the debt was paid back under the contract, the Farm Credit Corporation would be quite justified in getting an
June 1, 1981

interest in the additional profit. That is being done all the time in private business because businesses are caught in the same way as everybody else, including the farmer. They have to shift toward some type of equity financing on which there is no interest or some sort of an interest in their profit which has no interest on it as well.
My proposal is sensible. 1 use it all the time in private business and it works. No one loses under that system. There is no subsidy. The suggestion of the hon. member for Medicine Hat is so simple and obvious that grain farmers will put their money into those trust accounts.
Cattle farmers will put their money in and everybody who wishes he were a farmer would put his money in if he got the chance. They will not quarrel about the 6 per cent. If there is worry about the fact it will be in there for a long while, the interest could be indexed along with inflation to ensure the farmer does not suffer. Index the principal if you want. The fact remains that something practical has to be done, not next week but now.
These ideas have been put before this House for the past seven or eight years starting with the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the hon. member for Swift Current, the hon. member for Mackenzie and myself, to the then minister in charge of the Wheat Board who introduced the stabilization for grain, it was put forward then as a positive, simple alternative to help stabilize the farm income without any cost to the government. Keep the government out of it. Those proposals were passed over for this complicated, legalistic type of tax law that we got in the stabilization act. No one understands that law except the tax expert, and I sometimes have doubts about them.
I think 1 have driven home this point as well as I can. I do so not only on the basis that it makes good common sense. To go out and tell the farmer tomorrow that you are going to put this proposal before cabinet would shake this cabinet out of a year's growth. It would really smarten them up. If the minister says he is going to put it forward, and if cabinet cannot prove that it cannot be done without a shadow of a doubt, you are walking the plank and you are telling why. My God, they would come back from all over the world to make sure he does not walk it.
No one dismisses a minister of agriculture of this country without a revolution from one end of the country to the other as long as he is fighting on behalf of the farmer. It is something where you cut across party lines. Canada as it is with all its great diversity can only have one federal minister of agriculture. Sometimes he is from the west, sometimes from the east, but it cannot make any difference. He speaks for all the farmers. Regardless of what language he speaks or where he comes from and regardless of the difference of views of many farmers, as long as they know he is sticking up for them, they will forgive many of his blunders and mistakes. As long as you let them know you do not care what their politics are or where they come from and that they will get fair treatment, farmers will always back their federal minister of agriculture.
Adjournment Debate
Some of us can speak with great experience on that, having once gone against all the farmers. When they came around in a year or so, the support was overwhelming, regardless of political affiliation. They did not care that I was called Conservative because they knew that I stood up for them. With everyone against me-only one other member of the Conservative caucus supported me-I survived. I was not afraid. 1 did not want to be minister of agriculture anyway.
No prime minister is ever going to fire a minister of agriculture. If you really want to shake up the self-styled leaders of the nation who parade up and down as cabinet ministers today, just say that you were listening to this debate and you think there is a lot of sense in it. We are not asking for subsidies so the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will not be against you.
We are asking for a simple type of proposal whereby the farmer can put his money into some form of trust account. He will do it. All you have to tell a farmer is he will get out of taxes for a while and he will do anything. Get that money out at 6 or 8 per cent, whatever you can, just say you are going to do it and every farmer's hopes will rise again. If you say you are going to back him up and there will be no subsidy, no prime minister will turn you down. Think what a morale booster it would be for the Department of Agriculture. Instead of dragging along under this situation, catching hell from one end of the country to the other, they would have their minister finally speak up, saying he is willing to walk the plank if justice is not done to the agricultural industry. That is the challenge we put before the minister tonight.

(A)	QUERY RESPECTING AID FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
(B)	REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY ACTION
(C)	REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO BENEFIT WOMEN AGED 55 TO 65 YEARS

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, May 19, as recorded in Hansard at page 9674, I raised with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) the plight being faced by many senior citizens, and in particular I asked that something be done by

June 1, 1981
Adjournment Debate
way of making an increase in the old age pension on an emergency basis.
I asked in particular that the Minister of National Health and Welfare not tell us, as others on the government side do so often, about the $35 increase that was made last summer, because in point of fact that increase has been completely eaten up by increases in food and rental costs that senior citizens have had to meet. I also asked her not to try to make the point that that increase is fully indexed as though that takes care of the situation. I pointed out in fact that during the past year, when the over-all consumer price index has gone up by over 12 per cent, the actual increase in dollars in the total amount of the guaranteed income supplement has gone up by only 8.8 per cent.
The reason, of course, the indexing of old age pensions is always behind is that it is based on a formula that permits the department to go back a month and then three months behind that and compare that three-month period with the three months before that, with the result that when pensioners get an increase in their pensions, they are never getting an increase to help them meet the costs they are having to cope with right then. It is because of that situation, I contend, there should now be another emergency increase in the amount of the old age pension, whether it is added to the basic old age security or to the guaranteed income supplement.
The minister, of course, did the very things I asked her not to do. She reminded us of the $35 increase last year and told us about the quarterly indexing that is supposed to be up to date. These are myths that any senior citizen can disprove. Then she went on to point out that the plea we sometimes make for a special cost-of-living increase for old age pensioners related to the things that they actually have to buy would not be of much help because her department had done the arithmetic and had found out that over a ten-year period the difference would be about one percentage point or .1 percentage point per year.
I tried to make the point back to her that I was not talking about what happens on a ten-year basis, but about the difficulties that pensioners are facing right now. I contend that the case is very strong for an emergency increase in the old age pension right away, and I made a particular reference to needs of women between 55 and 65 who get no pension at all.
I know we are always told that there is not any money, and 1 know that my plea for a pension increase flies in the face of those in this House, especially to my right, who are forever asking for the government to cut expenditures. I remind the government and the House of a period I remember very well when the government was not spending money, in the depression of the 1930s, and the result was that things got worse and worse. I suggest if it were not for government money that is going into the pockets of people in the form of old age pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance, veterans' pensions and all these things, our economy today would really be in a tailspin. I suggest that far from it hurting the economy to put money into the pockets of people who will spend it on things they need, it would actually be a help to the
economy, and even the business interests that keep calling for cuts in government spending would be better off if our social programs were expanded.
I say tonight that I am sorry the minister took such a negative stand in response to my question. I still do not think that is the way she feels about these matters. I believe she wants to see pensions and other social benefits increased. I can understand her not being here tonight, but I see I do not even have the attendance of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Frith).
I gather that the one parliamentary secretary who is here at this moment is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Irwin), who will respond. I hope he will do so with a sense of justice and fair play to the senior citizens of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development

First, Mr. Speaker, it is a myth that it is going to be easier for senior citizens in the next while. It is going to get more difficult with inflation and high interest rates. I see the latest census report in the U.S., which will probably mirror ours, indicates that for the first time since 1950 there are as many Americans above the age of 30 as there are below that age. That means that we have a shrinking work force which must provide for the economic well-being of a mushrooming elderly population.
Now I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will be the first to admit, and I say this very subjectively, that the best social legislation has been the combination of Liberal-CCF-NDP legislation over the years, but I think it is going to be more and more difficult in these times to provide the necessary money. In the last campaign we had really only one monetary promise where money was going out with no return and that was in the area of social assistance, directed to the 1.2 million senior citizens eligible for old age security and the GIS. We kept that promise and it was very expensive. The hon. member says not to remind him of what was done, but it is a fact that we kept the promise and we put out a lot of money.
When the hon. member asked the question in the House, he stated that we had not indexed this properly, that it was only 8.8 per cent. I have checked this and that figure is for a nine-month period from July, 1980 to April, 1981. If we calculate it for a full 12-month period ending this July, it will be approximately 12 per cent, which means the single pensioner will get an additional $17 and a married pensioner $13. I know it is not enough, I know that we have to look first after the elderly and the pensioners in our society, but we are in very difficult times and that is all we can do at this particular stage in the development of our economy.
We are doing all we can for those over 65, and it was suggested by the hon. member that we go into those areas below 65, namely the single woman currently ineligible for old age security. I think he is right when he says that the Minister
June 1, 1981

of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) would do it if she could. She indicated a figure of approximately $730 million to do all those things she wanted to do, but I do not think she can. And I think she was quite forthright and truthful when she said in the House that the government is doing all it can to look after those over 65; it will be some time before we can look after those 55 to 65.
Mir. Knowles: By that time they will be 65.

speechtext: Well, within the last 20 years we have and are providing income housing, senior citizen housing, provincial assistance, old age security and the GIS. At its worst, things are much better now than they were 20 or 30 years ago, and there is some responsibility on our citizens to do some saving of their own for their future retirement. I do not think we can continuously put the debt on the young workers of this country and expect them to go out and produce and earn money and pay the income tax they will have to pay. This is a shared responsibility.

subtopic: ENERGY-EXPORTS OF NATURAL GAS TO UNITED STATES
ENERGY-EXPORTS OF NATURAL GAS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 13 I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) if he would consider a policy in which he would not allow any further exports of natural gas from Canada to the United States until there was a firm commitment by the gas transmission companies like TransCanada Pipelines to serve the underserved areas of eastern Canada.
The reason I asked the question was that I was not sure whether the transmission companies like TransCanada Pipelines and the distribution companies like Northern and Central Gas Corporation Limited, which serves northeastern and eastern Ontario, had any clear direction as to just how rapidly they would served the underserved areas of eastern Canada.
There is a program in the National Energy Program called the federal distribution system expansion program which provides grants for distribution of natural gas in these communities, but the cost of the transmission lines into many of these communities will be very high. I am not sure whether that whole grant system will be adequate to cover it. For instance, in northeastern and eastern Ontario there are some 150 communities which need service, and the assistance will have to come out of that program.
In my own constituency it is estimated that it will cost something like $80 million to put through the transmission gas pipeline, part of which will be borne by TransCanada Pipelines and part by the distribution company, supposedly Northern and Central Gas Corporation. The volume of gas probably will not be adequate to amortize the cost, so it is a question of grants or the cost of that gas pipeline being borne ultimately by the producers of natural gas in western Canada, if it is added to the rate base of TransCanada Pipelines.
If we look at it in the national perspective, we see some six billion cubic feet of gas being used per year. This displaces
Adjournment Debate
about one million barrels of oil. We are subsidizing oil to the extent of $20 per barrel through the compensation program. So we will see a net saving for the country of some $20 million just in the communities along the north shore of Lake Huron. It is clearly in the national interest.
Whether companies like TransCanada will move to put in transmission facilities is highly questionable. They will not actually move ahead with it, unless they are certain that their chances of exporting gas to the United States will be virtually zero. I am hopeful the minister will ensure that more exports will not be approved to the United States until the underserved areas of eastern Canada are provided with natural gas. This only makes sense. We are spending a great deal of money under the Canadian oil substitution program to convert furnaces from oil to natural gas.
Obviously those gas transmission lines and distribution systems should be in place before we can carry out the substitution. 1 am hopeful the minister will adopt a policy of no further exports until the areas in eastern Canada which are not presently served with natural gas pipelines are being served.
